speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: CANADIAN DEEP-SEA SHIPPING INDUSTRY- .QUESTION AS TO GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE

Well, Mr. Speaker, I am afraid I am not in a position to answer that question fully. Speaking generally I can say that the maritime commission have already put in motion the usual procedure to deal with the situation following the statement made in the house by the Prime Minister last December. I believe that early in December last they invited all ship operators and ship owners to forward their applications, indicating whether they wanted their ships transferred to the United Kingdom flag or whether they wanted to take advantage of the $3 million subsidy which was announced. I do not know whether my hon. friend has anything particularly in mind, but that is the general position as I know it.
The Prime Minister calls to my attention the fact, in addition to what I have said, that there is an item in the estimates to cover the amount of the subsidy.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yesterday afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I devoted my entire time to the consideration of several problems relating to the Sunchild Cree and Chippewa Indians located within my constituency. On that occasion, I laid emphasis upon the fact that as yet there is no indication whatever that the Department of National Health and Welfare appreciates the seriousness of the problem of health among these Indians. Moreover, there is no indication that appropriate steps have been instituted to meet, or even partly solve, the problem which exists.
In my opinion this results from one of two things. Either it is believed by some that this problem affects only a limited number of people, possibly removed from the well-beaten paths of the white man, or else government policy itself is such that justice cannot be rendered to these unfortunate people. In referring to policy I should like to quote from a statement made by the minister. I understand that this was in the form of a directive which was sent to certain of his departmental officials. It reads as follows:
While the dominion government has assumed specific obligations with respect to certain citizens, the only responsibility with respect to persons of native status is to organize a health program for those groups which are as yet unable to make s-uch arrangements independently. The officers of the Indian health services are charged with the responsibility of judiciously administering funds appropriated for this health program. It is not the intention to operate a complete but non-contributory service. The service now provided is certainly far in excess of that ever promised by implication.
I should like also to quote from a statement made by the director of Indian health services. He is even more specific. He said:
The federal government is under no obligation to supply free medical attention to any Indian.
This statement is in direct conflict with that of another departmental official, namely, Dr. Meltzer, medical director of the Charles Camsell Indian hospital in Edmonton. He said:
The health of Indians is our direct responsibility.
I would suggest that, when the Indian affairs committee meets, some members of the committee take up these statements and endeavour to get a clear-cut assertion of government policy and responsibility in this field. That is all I am going to say, Mr. Speaker, about Indian health services.
Yesterday I referred to other aspects of the problem falling within the purview of the department of Indian affairs. In concluding these remarks I just want to say that I should like to see immediate action taken to block out the timber I mentioned. I feel it is essential, and probably it will be done. I want
(Mr. Abbott.]

to see some supervision of the construction of those houses, and some expert advice provided for these Indians, in order that they may put under cultivation the land suitable for agricultural purposes. In this way food could be produced for the livestock which they now have, and must have in greater numbers if they are ever to become selfsupporting.
I should like to emphasize that obviously some people who deal with the Indians do not know that you cannot break faith with these people and expect to obtain the results which government policy should be designed to obtain. For example, you cannot tell the Indians to meet at a certain point on December 21 to receive certain parcels which are provided for them at Christmas, have them wait two or three days with no one showing up, have many of the parcels still undelivered a month later, and still expect the Indians to have faith. I know that a new Indian Act is to be brought down. I know also that it will take more than an act, it will take more than words, to deal effectively with such a long-standing problem as Canada's Indian problem. It is essential, Mr. Speaker, that along with the act there must be the proper spirit; there must be the will to do the right thing for these people. Above all we must cease to look upon the native population as an inferior people; that has been one of our principal difficulties.
I wish the new minister who is handling the Indian affairs branch all the luck in the world. I believe he will approach this problem in the right spirit. I trust that his desire to meet and solve the problems connected with the new Indian Act will result in a solution.
There is one other thing, Mr. Speaker, to which I should like to refer this afternoon. There is a reference to it in paragraph 3 of the speech from the throne, which reads as follows:
In the meantime negotiations are proceeding with the provincial governments for the implementation of the legislation adopted at your last session respecting housing, a transcontinental highway, and forest conservation.
It is to the trans-Canada highway that I wish to devote a few moments. This matter has always been an issue, but when it became a live issue it was very interesting to me to observe how quickly chambers of commerce, boards of trade, city and town councils, agricultural and other organizations got busy to plug for certain specific routes, especially in western Canada. New organizations came into being, and caravans began their weary trek across to the western coast in order to win support for specific routes, as well as to create on the part of the people who live in

those areas an interest in the matter. Tons of literature were printed and distributed across the country. As a matter of fact the battle of the route was actually fought, partly [DOT] at least, on the floor of this house.
My personal conviction with respect to this matter might be summarized in this way. First, defence and the economic welfare of Canada certainly demand that a trans-Canada highway be constructed without delay. Second, I was hopeful that this matter would never become a political football. Third, I was convinced in my own thinking that if the right thing were done, a factfinding body made up of provincial and federal representatives would immediately come into being. Of course my fourth view is that eventually, at least as to that part of the country from Winnipeg west, we would have a series of routes; that is, you would probably have upwards of four transcontinental highways.
One thing that has struck me-and this applies particularly to the route within my own province, or what might become the route-is that newspaper and other references have always been to the Crowsnest pass route, the Kicking Horse pass route or the Yellow-head pass route. The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) and others have plugged hard and consistently for the Crowsnest pass route. The hon. members for Medicine Hat (Mr. Wylie), Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) and Calgary West (Mr. Smith), have plugged for the Calgary-Banff route, the Kicking Horse pass route. The hon. members for Battle River (Mr. Fair), Vegreville (Mr. Decore), Edmonton East (Mr. Macdonald), Edmonton West (Mr. Prudham), Peace River (Mr. Low), and Athabaska (Mr. Dechene), have all plugged for the Yellowhead pass route. While I do not want to start the battle here again, it is amazing to me that all of them, in their anxiety to have the route pass through their own communities, have completely overlooked the fourth and most practical route of all, namely, the one that goes through what is now referred to as the David Thompson route.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), and the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson), could both advance strong arguments, I am sure, to show this house and the country why the trans-Canada highway should not go through the semi-arid, semi-desert areas in southern Saskatchewan and southeastern Alberta. I am sure they could give ever so many reasons why it should go through their constituencies after proceeding westward from Winnipeg. I am sure that the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) could give ever so many reasons why
The Address-Mr. Shaw that same route should pass through his constituency. If it does pass through these three, as it should, then it could not help reaching the city of Red Deer in the province of Alberta.

speechtext: Where is that?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Someone says: Where is Red Deer? Possibly I could answer that question by quoting from a short editorial which recently appeared in the Edmonton Bulletin:
Red Deer is one of the Alberta points to watch.
The city with the interesting past has a very promising future.
Strategically situated midway between Calgary and Edmonton, it is an ideal location to take advantage of the current trend to decentralize industry.
On many occasions in recent months Red Deer has been cited as an up-and-coming industrial centre, and faith in its future has been expressed by the dominion itself in announcement from Ottawa that it is going ahead with a $361,000 federal building.
May I just digress at that point, Mr. Speaker, to convey to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) and to the government the appreciation of all of the citizens of the city of Red Deer, and my own, of the fact that finally that great problem which does exist in the city of Red Deer has been recognized and is now to be met. We are pleased that a building of that size is to be constructed in that city. I continue the quotation:
Apart from its location and facilities, Red Deer is well able to take care of continued growth, for it is the centre of one of the most lush mixed farming areas in the province.
What a contrast that is to the constituency of the hon. member for Medicine Hat!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is one man's opinion.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The editorial continues:
Then too, it is the hub of a new highway into the Nordegg country of the foothills to the west.
Incidentally, Nordegg is one of the greatest steam coal producing areas in western Canada. I hope the Canadian National Railways and the government will soon begin to realize that fact. The editorial goes on:
Completion of the highway will tap rich natural resources of timber and coal for Red Deer's benefit.
It is expected the highway will continue west from Nordegg into the mountains to join the Banff-Jasper route, and, if that happens, Red Deer will find itself in a class with Edmonton and Calgary as a jumping-off place for the summer mountain tourist trade.
I still think it is ahead of them, but that is the opinion of the Edmonton Bulletin. Finally:
All told, Red Deer is out front as another good place to live in a good province.
That is the end of the Bulletin editorial. If one goes on west of the city of Red Deer he passes over one of the finest mixed farming parts of Canada into the town of Rocky

The Address-Mr. Shaw Mountain House. That name alone indicates to hon. members what lore must be associated with a town having such a name.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Especially "Rocky Mountain".

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
From Rocky Mountain House one travels over an area in which the province of Alberta today is in the process of constructing one of the finest highways to be found in that part of Canada. As I said before, you reach Nordegg, where the great Brazeau collieries produce a tremendous amount of bituminous coal for use in Canada's industrial life. From there westward this route would pass over the Kootenay plains. You have heard of tropical valleys, Mr. Speaker; British Columbia has boasted about them from time to time. Here we have the best example of what might be called a tropical valley in our Rocky mountains. These Kootenay plains are as flat as the prairie district. The temperature there is always fifteen to twenty degrees above that registered at points outside the pass. There is no snow in there at times when there are two feet of snow on the prairies to the east; and this road passes through to meet the Banff-Jasper highway. For forty-five miles beyond the Banff-Jasper highway the road would extend through the Howse pass, which is the lowest pass in the Canadian rockies, with an elevation of 4,840 feet. This area would be one of the easiest to keep free from snow in the wintertime and one of the least costly to construct. There is less snow in that area than in any other section of the Rocky mountains on the North American continent.
That is quite a contrast, Mr. Speaker, to the thirty feet of snowfall that you often find around west of Banff and Lake Louise. We still think-and these remarks are addressed to the government of Alberta as well as to the government of Canada-that if they are interested in establishing the trans-Canada highway where it will cost least to construct, where it will cost least to maintain, where we have natural beauty unexcelled on this continent, and where wildlife abounds in untold numbers; if they realize the advantages afforded by this route, coupled with the low elevation, there will be no question as to where the trans-Canada highway will run in that part of Canada.
I would say to the government of Canada and also to the government of Alberta that if this highway goes through Calgary, then Lethbridge and Edmonton will be offended. If it goes through Lethbridge you are going to offend the other two. If it goes through Edmonton it will also offend the other two. We do not mind offending all these cities-

not a bit. We feel that if the governments involved do not want to offend just two of them they will hasten to accept the route .which I have mentioned as the logical one for the trans-Canada highway. We feel that one could give this government and the provincial government the best possible arguments and support for such a decision. My personal hope is that eventually all the four cities which I have mentioned will find themselves on trans-Canada routes, because beyond question eventually from Winnipeg west we must have at least the four routes to which I have referred.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by following the pleasant practice of congratulating the mover (Mr. Larson) and the seconder (Mr. Dumas) of the motion for an address to His Excellency the Governor General on their performance of the duties allotted to them. It is one of the pleasant things about democracy that, however much we may differ on principles, we are able to practise these amenities; and I might particularly say that this amenity can be practised today when we see the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) back in his seat. However much we may differ with him, we are glad to see him here. We can assure him that his name has not been wholly forgotten; that there have been frequent references to him, some of which have been highly eulogistic and some not so eulogistic.
This afternoon I wish to bring to the attention of the house the question of foreign exchange control as it exists in the western world, by which I mean the non-communist world. I believe, though it is a subject that we have treated in the past with a good deal of perfunctoriness, it will not be hard to convince this house today that it is a matter of great importance to us all.
Foreign exchange control first of all came to us as a war guest. It was hoped and expected that, like other war guests which were more welcome than foreign exchange control, it might leave us at the end of the war. But then it was continued. It really was introduced into what I might call the financial family with a kind of legal status, in spite of the fact that its parentage was deplorable, ns I shall show later. It almost seems as if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) now can hardly distinguish between this child, as I say of deplorable parentage, and the more respectable members of his family.
I hope that in the circumstances in which we find ourselves now we may be able to have this child sent off to the place where it originated, namely, the totalitarian countries, and that it may flourish there as best it can.

Of course it has developed a veneer of good manners, but that should not blind us as to its real quality.
I want to bring before the house this afternoon four considerations. First I wish to satisfy the house-and it should not be difficult-that we are suffering from exchange control now; that the fetters which tie the non-communist countries are dividing it into two areas, with the dollar-sterling curtain in between; that in a sense they are driving us back to barter; they are depriving us of the progress of centuries.
Second, I wish to deal particularly with the devaluation that took place last autumn, and seek to convince the house that devaluation is not enough; that devaluation without freedom will not alone do the job.
Third, I wish to convince the house that if every nation waits until everyone is ready we may wait until it is too late; and I hope we in Canada, who are often fond of talking about the value of our example, may be able to give some kind of example here.
Finally, I wish to argue that we are in a favourable position to do so.
This is not the first time that I have attempted to interest the government in this question, but in the past I have been unsuccessful. When people are prosperous, when everyone has his pockets full of money, when he believes that everything is for the best in the best of all possible worlds, it is very hard to get him to believe that any clouds can arise on the horizon at all; but I think the difficulties are now beginning to emerge. So far as I can understand, it is not very difficult to persuade the farmers that not everything is still good. Take just one other industry to which I shall refer later; I think the newsprint manufacturers may have something to say about the difficulties which exchange control is causing them.
I hope to be able to satisfy the house and the government that the villain in the piece in both these cases, and in others as well, is the foreign exchange control measures which are spread all over the so-called free world, and which are getting in the way of those who are trying to carry on business. I hope that now that the farmers and the industrial workers can accept that, even the government may accept it.
Crooning to the farmers has gone out of fashion since last spring, and we no longer live in that pleasant Never-Never land where Peter Pan lived and where he never had to grow up. I think we are growing up. I think the government is showing signs of

The Address-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell learning things. The government learned between Monday and Wednesday of last week that there was unemployment in the land. On Monday we had the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), which really made one wonder whether it was not almost indecent to suggest that there was any unemployment at all, so insinuatingly, so persuasively, so almost absent-mindedly he spoke of unemployment, as if it really was not here at all, or if it was it was just an accident of the climate, and that it would disappear with the spring when the birds come again. Well, on Wednesday, a few days later, apparently they had a change, because the debate on the address had to be invaded for the second or third time in order that the unemployment insurance measure could be carried through-and it was a very good thing it was carried through, though the surprising thing is that the Prime Minister did not know on Monday that it should be. Therefore, as I say, I have hopes for the government, and of course the hopes are accentuated by the return of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and by the foreword which appeared in the morning papers as to his arrival.
I am reading from the Montreal Gazette which carries a headline reading: "Howe predicts more exports." This headline rang a bell in my memory. I looked back and I found that on May 9, 1949, there was a similar headline in the Ottawa Citizen which read: "New deal disclosed by Howe." That was on May 9. That is what you might call an election sweetener. We read lower down that the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that he had negotiated contracts to the total value of $25 million. That is not a very large amount in the face of the whole of our trade; nevertheless there it was for what it was worth.
It is interesting to turn back to what the Minister of Trade and Commerce told them in New York yesterday. He explained that he was on a holiday during which time he "made efforts to encourage some countries to increase their exports to Canada." Then he says this:
The over-all outlook tor Increased1 trade with Europe is improving all the time.
That is good. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), I know, will be very glad to hear that. In fact it is a pity he did not know it a little earlier. The minister goes on and says:
Canada was encouraging private businessmen to arrange barter deals-
I suppose if we cannot have trade we can barter. If we cannot have real trade we have

The Address-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell to barter. It seems a pity we have to go back to the past like that. Next the minister said:
We are encouraging such deals because we want to make it as easy as possible for private trade to function.
Then at the end of the interview occurs this, which I find encouraging too. At the end of the interview the writer said:
Mr. Howe is returning to Ottawa tomorrow where, he said, he faces "a few routine things to get back to."
Now, I think the minister may find when he finds out what has happened here that some of the things are not so routine as he might have thought. He will not find unemployment quite so routine. Nevertheless it is a good thing to have him back, because he is always so optimistic; of course he tries to make everyone feel that this government is an all-wise government. Certainly the Prime Minister has gone a long way toward suggesting that the Minister of Trade and Commerce at all events does have that qualification.
I said a moment ago that we were suffering from the shackles of foreign exchange control, and I should like to read one or two statements in support of that. I would like to read the familiar words of the Minister of Agriculture, from what he said in December last in Brantford. I shall read a short extract in advance of that, something he said on May 28 last. He told an audience in Winnipeg that what we needed was "more food products to sell".
That was on May 28. But by December 1 he was telling the farmers that they would have to buy where they could sell, and he went on to declare:
The only place we can sen freely for the time being is Canada.
He suggested that we will have to sell in Canada; but it will be quite a task for Canadians to eat as much wheat as would take care of the Saskatchewan crop. Nevertheless that is what the minister suggested.
We all remember what the minister said in this House of Commons a short time ago, that there was a deliberate onslaught by the British government-and it will be noted it was the British government, not the British people-a deliberate onslaught on Canadian trade.
I should like to carry this one step further by saying what has happened to Canadian newsprint. As I recall, we had a contract for roughly 300,000 tons of Canadian newsprint. Canadian newsprint manufacturers had supplied Britain for years when it was inconvenient for them to do so, and at a price less than that at which the British 
could buy it elsewhere. The British importers were keen to continue the contracts, but in January, two months ago, the British government advised them that they could give no import permit for a period of six months, and that they were not able to give an assurance as to what would happen after that time.
I do not think anyone imagines that the British government are doing that out of malice or as a prank. The truth of the matter is that the British government, like other governments, are caught in this maze of controls which support overvalued currencies by rigid controls and rationing of foreign exchange.
It has been, so far, extraordinarily difficult to get people to buckle down to the task of taking this problem seriously, and if it was not for the fact that we are now finding ourselves in difficulties we would not get people to take it seriously even yet.
Controls are everywhere-import controls; export controls; controls of all kinds. It is in the air. Of course Great Britain in 1949 was the classic case. Every knowledgeable person except the Chancellor of the Exchequer knew that the pound was being dealt in at a figure far below the fixed rate, and eventually the Chancellor of the Exchequer had to come to devaluation; but there was no relaxation of the tightness of the controls. All that happened was that $2.80 was substituted for $4.03. In that connection I would like to read a sentence from the London Economist. Hon. members will realize that the London Economist is not only sympathetic but generous in its attitude toward the government. It sympathizes largely with' the objectives of the British government. It says this about devaluation in its issue of October 15, 1949:
It is now clear that the opportunity of devaluation has been missed. Abroad, there has been much disappointment, mixed with amazement, that so sharp a reduction in the exchange value of the pound sterling was not accompanied by the relaxation whatsoever of the restrictions that keep the pound so tightly inconvertible. "Devaluation," says one experienced continental commentator, "is usually the price paid for getting rid of exchange control. To pay so high a price and get none of the reward is a very bad business."
Now, as I have said, all the old powers have been maintained. There is, however, one hopeful sign; it is the fact that New Zealand and Australia have turned their faces away from controls. And in England last week the election returns could not be regarded as an enthusiastic endorsement of them.
Of course we must not overlook the great difficulties which England has. We must not overlook the three and a quarter billion

pounds of indebtedness they have. We must not overlook the fact that they spent such vast proportions of their resources in the carrying on of the war. But in addition to that there is and has been a doctrinaire mentality at work there. While tentative attempts have been made to introduce freedom to facilitate foreign investment, all that has happened is the substitution of one labyrinth of red tape for another: In the meantime the life-giving stream of foreign investments has remained cut off.
What, in plain words, is foreign exchange control? It means this: that the government of a country fixes in terms of its own currency the value of other currencies; then it enforces that rate upon the public, upon its own citizens, backed by the police power of the state, so that the citizens of the state can deal only at this fixed rate.
Those police powers you may recall. I do not wish to take too much time, but I should like to read one or two of the more extreme powers. They state:
The governor in council may make regulations prescribing that persons who would otherwise be residents shall be deemed to be non-residents or that persons who would otherwise be non-residents shall be deemed to be residents for any of the purposes of this act.
I have always understood that the British parliament had powers to do everything except to make a man a woman, or a woman a man. But this section seems almost to go beyond that. Then there is this one further subsection I should like to read. Regulations may be made:
Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained elsewhere in this act. exempting any person or any class of persons or any transaction or class of transactions from any provisions of this act.
In other words this body, the governor in council, is given the absolute power to deal in any way it pleases. Let me add quickly that I think those powers have been, on the whole, exercised with judgment and with moderation. The fetters, so to speak, have been softened. Nevertheless there is the power. And let us never forget this: that when all other controls are done away with but foreign exchange control is left, it is the control of all controls. So long as the government can control arbitrarily every transaction in which any foreign money is involved, it has virtually complete control-an astonishing amount of power.
When one couples that with the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act, there is virtually nothing that cannot be done. Tomatoes and lettuce are "off again, on again". We never know whether we can have them or not from day to day. Perhaps we should learn something more about the tastes of the Minister

The Address-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce-their own personal tastes in foods-so that we could try to forecast just how these things will be dealt with.
In plain words, every transaction, no matter how small, has to have a permit, and one's personal business becomes the business of the board. If you wish money to go to the United States, you must lay bare your affairs. If you wish to move to the United States, they have the right to ask why you are doing it-whether you are moving away from your mother-in-law, or what. They have the right to examine into your affairs and be satisfied in their judgment as to what should be done. If you wish to send a few pounds to Great Britain, you have to satisfy them that it is necessary, because they have this policing power. We tried hard to have some relaxation, but we were told four years ago that it was a case of whole hog or none. Is it any wonder that a distinguished citizen of this country described the measure as being a peacetime measure "which was unnecessary and one which interfered with the basic rights of Canadian citizens"? That was said by Senator Crerar in the Senate in 1946. Senator McGeer gave an amusing description of the permit power in the Senate when he said that you could not take a suitcase of personal effects across the line without a permit. Another senator said that if you wanted to abide strictly by the permit system you would have to cross the frontier in a state of nature.
What about the origin of this foreign exchange control? I said that it had a deplorable ancestry, and I shall try to substantiate that. Like the mule, it has no pride of ancestry, and I would hope it has no hope of posterity. We first heard of its being used by the bolsheviks in 1917; but the man who is the real inventor, the man who should be given the real honour, is Schacht, of Germany, who brought it in in the early thirties. I need not tell you that this was the key control, which, added to other controls, enabled Hitler, plus Schacht, plus the Gestapo to make all their preparations for war. If we may use the language of the racetrack, we may say that foreign exchange control was by Schacht out of Gestapo.
There have been other attempts to control international prices. Hon. members will recall the efforts in connection with rubber and coffee. I read a report in the press the other day which explained why the price of coffee had shot up. According to this report the reason was quite simple. The price was controlled, and then millions of coffee trees were taken out of production, with the result that there is not enough coffee to go round
384	HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Address-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell and the price has gone up. I say nothing of the hardship to the persons involved-mainly, no doubt, small producers.
What I do wish to say is that it is just too hard for a few individuals to foresee the consequences of these far-reaching actions. If human beings were robots; if we were all economic men who moved according to mechanical rules, possibly there might be more to be said for it. But when you take human beings, each with his own desires and his own feelings as to how he will regulate his life, then when other people try to regulate it, it is a failure.
How much more difficult is it to regulate the price of a thing like money, which affects every commodity in the community, which enters into every detail of our life. How much more difficult is it to do that. It is not too much to say that this arrogant assumption of supreme wisdom always ends in disaster. When I say "arrogant assumption" I am not referring to those officials who have been carrying out the terms of this act; I am referring only to the general principle which inspires foreign exchange control and which I hope we may have the wisdom at least to begin to get rid of.
Of course exchange control has its friends. First of all there are people who are convinced that controls are right; there are people who believe in them. These are people whom I respect, although I believe their views are wholly wrong. I respect them because they are honest about their views; they say: Yes, we are going to control you ; look out! I always hope that the kindly light of reason may invade their minds and one day they will drop those views; nevertheless there they are, and they are entitled to them.
But there is another and very different class of people whom I do not admire nearly so much. These are the people who proclaim constantly their adherence to freedom but who as a matter of fact like controls in their own affairs very much indeed. I am not going to go further on that except to relate to the house a little incident that came to my attention through a wise banker friend. He was talking during the war with an importer who told him what a happy life he was having. He said to the banker: "My imports come in at a fixed price; I sell them at a fixed price, and there is a pleasant spread between.
I have no reason to worry about foreign exchange, because it is sold at a fixed price.
I am able to shut up my office door about midday and go off and play golf". My banker friend made a very wise reply to him. He said: "You know what has happened, you are no longer in business". I think that tells the whole story.

I am fond of quoting the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) on this. He said something in this house with which I have always agreed and which I like to repeat: "I do not object to private enterprise, but if they are going to take the profits, they have to take the risks as well". I would not want it to be thought that I am quoting the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar as the embodiment of divine wisdom, but I think that one statement was sound, and I should like to quote it to those who in my opinion are the worst enemies of freedom that you can find, because they proclaim themselves as being its friend when their actions give them away.
I should like to try to relate this specifically to our special difficulty with the United Kingdom. Why is it that we are losing markets and fear the further loss of markets in the United Kingdom? Of course it would be difficult if the pound were fully convertible. Then the people in the United Kingdom would be able to spend their money as they liked and where they liked. They would be able to buy wheat or anything else they wanted in this country, provided that the price was right. I am not going to suggest that convertibility would produce a miracle overnight, but I am suggesting that it would begin the cure.
I am suggesting that we are in danger- from this maze of controls. I shall support this by quotations; that things are going badly and there is no reason to expect that they will go any better. Incidentally I noticed in the annual report of the Royal Bank of Canada, issued the other day, a very wise remark by the president. He said that the real excuse for controls had gone now, that European production was up to the prewar level. I understand that it is practically up to the pre-war level in agricultural production, and fifteen per cent above it in manufacturing production. In the face of this, consider the situation in England today, six months after devaluation. Apparently there is little or no money available for agricultural products from North America. Apparently there is no money for newsprint. What is the money used for? It is used to buy exclusively North American products, such as Virginia tobacco and films. That is not said in criticism of Great Britain; that is said in criticism of this system which has us all shackled and which we must get rid of.
Of course even if the pound went free tomorrow it would not suddenly give them all kinds of United States dollars, but it would begin the cure. As I said before, it would begin to liberate the stream of investment which would begin to flow in and correct the

present situation. At the present time competent economists will tell you that they wonder whether anything else will do the job; whether anything else can span the dollar gap.
The bitterest irony of this control which is supposed to be our salvation is that it cuts us off from the very thing which could begin to provide the cure-international investment. There have been, as I said a moment ago, attempts to bring about some kind of freedom of investment in England. I think they have changed the number of years after which you can take money out, or something of the kind. It is just one bit more of red tape which the businessman must cut when he wants to invest. A businessman does not want to have to deal with government officials; he wants to deal with other businessmen. Unless there is some great lure like western oil, they are not going to invest except where there is freedom.
Do not let us forget that this whole control system is only twenty years old, whereas we had scores or hundreds of years of the other system. During all that time, when the world was still civilized, we had none of this. Lest anyone say: Yes, while we may have had stability before the war, there was also from time to time great hardship on certain people, when adjustments had to be made. I will admit that there is some truth in that, but I say that with the new techniques we have, with our new attitude toward and belief in social welfare, those difficulties would be taken care of. Merely because those difficulties exist we should not resign ourselves to the evils of controls.
You have been listening to one who certainly does not set himself up as an expert, and I should like to call in one or two experts, as they said on the radio program "Information Please." I should like to read just a sentence or two from a report by a body which has been criticized in this house, the international monetary fund, but was eulogized the other day by a competent hardheaded banker, namely, the president of the Royal Bank. When a hard-headed banker eulogizes a body of this kind and at the same time indicates that he is an advocate of freedom, I think it is worthy of note. I should like to read from the report; it is short, and I would ask hon. members to listen very carefully.
The members of the fund-
This was in April, 1949.
-have the obligation to put into effect as soon as possible such measures as are likely at the same time to improve their payments position and make possible the gradual reduction and ultimate elimination of restrictions on payments and transfers for current international transactions.
The Address-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell
Then it says this:
There are evident risks of various kinds in accepting the more competitive conditions that must follow such a policy; but unless these risks are accepted, the improvement in the world economic situation made thus far may be replaced by deterioration.
I suggest that is an understatement. We need not say it may be replaced by deterioration; we can say it is being replaced by deterioration. Then it goes on:
If the earliest reasonable opportunity is not seized to modify restrictive policies, the difficulty of resuming trade on an economic basis under more normal conditions will be greatly increased and world trade will tend more and more to be conducted with inconvertible currencies on the basis of bilateral bargains.
Again the report says:
The revival of the flow of private international capital, which is essential if the best use is to be made of the world's productive resources, is moreover scarcely to be expected if more elaborate exchange restrictions increasingly limit the uses to which earnings from foreign investments can be put.
It is of interest that yesterday, March 1, 1950, was the day which under the articles of agreement the fund was to report to its members on the restrictions in force at that time. In other words, after three years of operation, there was to be a sort of stocktaking or review of the situation.
I would call the attention of hon. members to four things from what I have read: first, the duty to get away from restrictions; second, the deterioration that will come about if we do not do so; third, acceptance of the fact that there is risk-but our whole system depends upon risk; only when there is risk is there incentive to call forth the maximum of effort on the part of people with energy and initiative. Fourth and last of all, they stress the importance of international investment.
If we need to underline the truth of these statements, let us carry our minds back three years, to 1947. What happened then? Two things happened. The British failed to make the pound convertible; and the Geneva treaty was negotiated, which has been almost ineffective except so far as Canada and the United States are concerned.
I have referred to the statement by the president of the Royal Bank. He has two things to say. He points to Britain's debt difficulty, and indeed suggests that the rest of the world should come to her assistance because the burden she bears was incurred in behalf of everyone. Then he calls for a period of freedom of exchange, for a certain fixed period when we should let the market determine rates of exchange as it did immediately after the first world war. Then he thinks we might work toward a period of stability, such as we had previously.

The Address-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell
Now I should like to sum up in a word. A few moments ago I said that devaluation last autumn was of some value; but was not enough. I quoted what I regard as three competent authorities; the international monetary fund itself, the London Economist, and the president of the Royal Bank. If the prospect is disturbing now, Mr. Speaker, is it likely to be any better when we come to the end of the Marshall plan? In congratulating ourselves on what has been going on, we have often forgotten to mention the enormous extent to which the Marshall plan and its various ancillary bodies have helped the situation.
Is this exchange problem going to remain with us forever? Is the minister going to keep this doubtful child in his financial family in spite of its deplorable origin, or is he going to expel it?
What prevents a return to freedom? First of all there is pride. I have never been a member of the government, though there are always hopes; but I have no doubt a government develops pride. There is unwillingness to admit that anything done by the government can be wrong. One member of the government, however, does not seem to be clothed with pride in the matter. I refer to the Minister of Agriculture; and I want to quote something he said just over a year ago, speaking in London, because I think it so true:
X am convinced that the world is not in any state of mind where it can be expected to agree that the manipulation of any system or systems of currency is going to be allowed to interfere with the will of those who have empty stomachs when it is preventing their purchasing surpluses of food and distributing them.
I suggest that is exactly what is happening now, that the manipulations of currency are preventing that very thing; and I suggest to the minister that he bring this situation to the attention of his colleagues. I think that was a wiser remark than the reference by the Prime Minister to chaos. Chaos is a word that covers a great deal of territory, one of those words we all use without perhaps intending very much. The Prime Minister used it on June 6 of this year in Quebec, when, speaking of devaluation, he said:
That would bring chaos to the Canadian economy in twelve months or so.
It might be interjected by the Minister of Finance, so I shall do it myself, that when the Canadian devaluation was made last autumn it was done at a time when other currencies were devalued. However, as I was saying, there is pride in this connection; and no doubt the Prime Minister, remembering his use of the word "chaos", might find difficulty in changing his view.


But there i^ another and, I think, more real difficulty. Government officials have been administering all these controls; and I want to say quite candidly that I think they have made the best of a bad job. But those who have been administering controls really have an extraordinary intellectual job to do in order to conclude that the time has come to abandon them. It seems to me they almost have to jump out of their intellectual skins, and that presents a difficult problem. Meanwhile, the abnormal is becoming the normal. I am sure they feel what I quoted from Senator Crerar was like a voice from another world. It has become respectable now to have controls. The day before yesterday the minister himself referred to the orders issued this year as compared with those of last year; and very naturally, I suppose, made the reference in such a way that he did not give me the impression of having the slightest feeling that these were things that we should get away from.
I have pointed to the effect of devaluation alone, and have shown that it has been largely sterile so far as we are concerned. I have quoted the advice given our farmers by the Minister of Agriculture, to sell at home. I have shown that this rigid control is preventing the flow of investment, which I think is the best hope we have for the future. It may be said in reply that we have had quite a lot of investment in Canada; nevertheless, to me that is no proof that fixed rates do not militate against investment. After all, there were strong reasons for investing here; and if anyone presents the argument that investments have been made in Canada, in spite of controls, it is perfectly open to me or any other member to say that such investments would have been much greater if there had been no such controls. When you consider Britain, you do not have the same sort of magnet for investment; nevertheless you have a concentrated market of forty-five million people, and I am assured by business friends that they believe investment would be freely made in Britain if the world could get away from these shackles.
I said a while ago, Mr. Speaker, that if we wait we may wait too long; and that brings me to the suggestion I wish to make. Why can we not make a start here? After all, we have had a considerable amount of experience since last September. I believe the official rate is endorsed by the rate on the dollar in the free market, such as it is; the dollar is quoted within a fraction of the ninety cents which is the official rate. Thirty years ago we took the risks, such as they were. We have a tremendously stronger position now, both absolutely and relatively. We have the added strength of iron ore and oil, which have

greatly improved our position. Actually in the last four months of the year we increased our exchange position by something like $130 million. As a matter of fact, as someone has said, at that time we were really supporting the United States dollar to that extent. We have no huge internal debt problem, as they have in England. I suggest that now is the strategic moment. We have evidence that in Australia, New Zealand and Great Britain, the control mind is not so firmly in the saddle. I am not suggesting that the freeing of the Canadian dollar is going to work any magic, any more than the freeing of the British pound at this moment would work any magic. After all, there is no mystery or magic involved. All I am asking is what Churchill suggested, that the government get out of the way, and let the millions of people who want to buy and sell to each other exercise their initiative, energy and ingenuity, without being forced to get permits for everything.
If, on the other hand, we do nothing, then the forest of controls becomes more and more deep-rooted. If the government, or the board, with its knowledge which the rest of us do not have concerning capital deposits, sees fit to begin with freedom on current account only, I would be disappointed; nevertheless I would say that was a beginning. Let us have a beginning. I would also say, let us not underestimate our own influence. In my opinion we are sometimes inclined to overestimate it, but I do not think we should underestimate it. I believe we have a place in the world. The fact that we are next door to the United States strengthens that place. Our action might give a lead which would prove fruitful.
As I was saying before the minister came in, yesterday served as a sort of stocktaking day, in which the present position of controls was to be investigated.
The minister made a speech last autumn somewhere in the United States, which I read with interest. He stated, with pardonable pride I thought, that two things have been characteristic of the policy of the Department of Finance-boldness and a sense of timing. The minister will forgive me if I say that we on this side of the house relate the timing rather to the election. We have done that before, so I need not stress that point. Last year we told the minister that we thought he was influenced by the political cycle rather than the economic cycle. But seriously I commend those two things to the minister-boldness and a sense of timing. I do suggest to him that now may be the moment when our action might have a real influence. I hope that we shall not have one day to make the devastating confession, "too little and too late."

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate this afternoon, realizing that it is the common practice of members to take advantage of this opportunity to tell something of their constituencies, I hope that my constituents, as well as hon. members, will not feel that it is a lack of interest or pride in my constituency that has deterred me from making an earlier address. I have waited until the second session of this twenty-first parliament primarily because, in common with the other members on this side of the house, I was genuinely interested in allowing sufficient time to consider the estimates and legislation that were before us l&st fall during a necessarily short session.
I wish to congratulate the mover (Mr. Larson) and seconder (Mr. Dumas) on their addresses, which precipitated this debate. They did an excellent job. They will probably get little satisfaction from any complimentary remarks that a new member extends, but I do wish to add my compliments to those already given. If I attempt to cover as many points as I wish in this debate, the house may be suspicious that I intend to leave again to join a convention. I should like to assure the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), who so eloquently informed you of my absence last year, that I have a genuine interest in what is taking place.
The constituency I have the honour to represent, Kootenay East, comprises a large portion of the southeast corner of the province of British Columbia. There are three great valleys of the Kootenay and great Columbia rivers. These rivers drain almost the entire northerly portion of the Canadian Rockies. One might almost say there were three great Fraser valleys rolled into one, and bounded by mountains filled with coal and mineral wealth. The Columbia valley in the northern part of my riding is one that is particularly noted for its tourist attractions. There is also some mining and agriculture carried on there. In the Creston valley, we have a fruit industry-I was about to say thriving, but later on you will understand why I cannot say it is a thriving industry- as well as many tourist attractions.
The adjacent Kootenay lake is a mecca for sportsmen from all over the country. Cran-brook is in the centre of the riding, and is particularly noted for its tourist attractions, and as a logging and railway centre. It is situated on the celebrated Crowsnest pass railway, and is also on the north-south highway which extends to the tourist attractions I have already mentioned, as well as Banff and Lake Louise. The coal fields of the Crowsnest pass and the Fernie area contribute a great deal of wealth to the interior
388	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Byrne of the province. It is regrettable that because of the severe winter, which made it difficult to obtain coal cars, there has been a considerable amount of unemployment in that area. The people are struggling along however, and with the help of unemployment insurance payments I believe they are getting by. The mines will soon return to full-time operations.
I have purposely left until the last the city of Kimberley, which is my home. Although I am not going to describe the city itself,
I wish to point out what industries are there, and then continue with some of the points I have in mind concerning social security. In Kimberley is located the largest lead-zinc mine in the world. Ten thousand tons of ore roll from its portals daily, and the resultant 800 to 1,000 tons of concentrates, which are shipped to the Trail smelter in Kootenay West, provide employment for approximately 6,000 people; about 2,000 people in Kimberley, and I believe in excess of 4,500 in the Trail area. It certainly contributes a great deal to the well-being of Kootenay West. I might say that, in effect, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and I would be virtually without a riding if it were not for the Sullivan mine.
As I am on my feet for the purpose of discussing the speech from the throne, I must spend a certain amount of time on it. I am no economist, however; but because of my work in the past few years, dealing specifically with wages, sales and so on, I have necessarily gained a certain amount of information with regard to economics and have necessarily put myself in a position in which I can at least form an opinion and be prepared to agree or disagree with whatever arguments may be advanced.
In their complaints with regard to the throne speech, the opposition have contended that nothing has been done to ensure markets for our farm produce and insist that there are no measures taken to obviate the unemployment. Many members from this side of the house, including the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard), have defended the throne speech successfully in the matter of farm products. I simply wish to make a few observations. I feel that up to the present time the marketers of the main farm produce such as wheat, beef, pork, poultry and dairy products have not suffered a great deal. The gross income in 1948 was $2,449 million; for 1949 it was $2,409 million. The higher figure was for 1948 and the lower figure was for 1949; that latter figure shows a $40 million decrease or one and one-third per cent, which is far from the sixteen per cent that I have been hearing mentioned in this house since the opening of this session.


Considerable discussion has taken place with regard to the fact that farm prices were pegged during the war and for some years following it. Certainly during the war wages were also pegged, and we had little quarrel with that policy of the federal government. The controls were necessary, and I think that we may be congratulated that we wound up by not going into the tailspin which has taken place in areas where prices have been allowed to inflate themselves.
I have figures from the bureau of statistics which prove that at the present time, taking the 1926 figure as 100 per cent, farm prices are still, as of the end of 1949, nine points above the prices of whole or partially-manufactured articles. Those who work in manufacturing industries are primarily interested in this matter. These figures would tend to prove that labour's rates are still eight or nine points below farm prices for the same year.
There is, however, one group of farmers who seem to have been entirely forgotten; I refer to the apple growers of central British Columbia. For the 1949 crop they have, up to the present time, received little if any returns. I have already mentioned Creston valley. In that locality a large number of farmers now face what I may describe as near disaster because of the fact that for the apple crop, although it was somewhat larger than normal, markets have dropped off. The apple growers are therefore facing disaster if something is not done to assist them.
To build up a producing orchard takes from six to seven years. The land on which these orchards are planted, and the surrounding land, we might say, costs in the neighbourhood of $1,000 to $2,000 per acre. It is impossible for the tree fruit rancher to have on his farm a subsidiary product on which he can rely if his tree fruits fail. The mixed farmer has something to fall back on if one of his products fails to bring in a return. I think we can confidently say that those who are raising wheat in the central plains have found that, with the improvements in methods, and with the introduction of larger and better machines, they have been able to lower their production costs. With the fruit farmer, however, the situation is different.
Fruit farming does not lend itself to mechanization. Everything must be done by hand. The wage rates that are being paid at the present time, which are correct and proper, necessarily cause an extra amount of expense. The improvement in marketing methods has brought about the necessity for more handling which entails more labour charges at every turn. In the orchard the work goes on for twelve months of the year. If the winter is open, or even in a severe

winter, the fruit rancher is out pruning his orchard. In the spring he must begin spraying early, putting on a coat of spray. If it rains that day, he must return to the orchard and put on another coat. Perhaps throughout the summer almost innumerable sprayings will take place. There is also the matter of hand thinning. The apples must be thinned. Millions and millions of apples in one orchard must be handled by hand, taking them from the bud in order to allow large apples to mature. The picking must certainly be done by hand. So far there is no mechanization in the apple-picking industry. I have seen attempts made, but nothing has been accomplished; because the apple coming from the orchard must be without a blemish. If there is one spot on it, it is culled; and the consumer apparently does not want it. It will therefore be seen that the apple growers' costs are rising.
This year they are in this position; they have invested this money. The apples are in the packing houses, prepared for shipment, but no markets are available. The tree fruit board have attempted, somewhat generously I would say, to do something about a large portion of the surplus that the growers are going to have. We realize that if these apples are left, they will rot and must be dumped. It is different with wheat which may be stored and kept for even hundreds of years, if necessary, but certainly for a year or two until the market has levelled off and the producers are able to sell at prices which will at least pay the cost of production and give them some return. But they are facing this condition. As I under-stand it, the British Columbia tree fruit growers have offered to give a certain amount of their crop to Great Britain. The people of Canada who are doing fairly well economically should not allow this to be done without giving some support to these fruit growers. I would expect the hon. members who represent [DOT] farming constituencies to lend all support to a plea to the federal government to do something to help these tree fruit growers who are in this precarious position at the present time.
With regard to the unemployment situation, it is regrettable that we have some 350,000 unemployed in Canada. There are many factors which contribute to this situation, probably not the least of which is the present :oal shortage arising from the strikes in effect in the United States at the present time. Also the severe winter that we have experienced out west has had something to do with it. Even though the weather has been considerably milder in the east, it is not conducive at the present time to starting Large-scale construction or building. The building of the trans-Canada highway and
The Address-Mr. Byrne the national housing scheme should alleviate the situation. If it does not I am sure there is no hon. member on this side of the house who will go back to his constituency until he is assured that something has been done by the federal government authorities, if necessary, to support some project. If they do not start it themselves I am sure they will see to it that something is started in collaboration with the provincial authorities. We will not go home to our constituencies in the summer until we are sure that the situation has been controlled.

speechtext:
In India there is no unemployment; but in that country the scythe has not yet displaced the sickle. In Australia the motorcar is hardly known even amongst what you might call the middle class. The worker does not think of owning an automobile. In China, where the ox pulls the wooden plow which tills the field, there is no unemployment. In Egypt the treadmill lifts the water from the Nile. We could even take Great Britain, where they take the voters to the polls in stage coaches.
I know that some hon. member are becoming bored. They expected me to speak on the question of social security. I wish to say a word on the measures of social security that have been attained in Kimberley. In so doing I may attempt, and I hope hon. members will forgive me, to prove to the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) that while I was an unpaid elected representative of labour I had considerable success in that field. Incidentally the hon. member from time to time makes reference to me as one who claims to be a representative of labour.
I wish to remind the hon. member that while sitting in this house I do not claim to represent any one particular group of people in my constituency. I represent the employees, the farmer, the smaller businessman in retail and service capacity, the employers of labour, the unemployed, the aged and infirm. Certainly it is my bounden duty to be assured that the money collected from these various groups is spent prudently and, above all, to guard against the necessity for any increase in the present heavy burden of taxation. Certainly I do not think we should use it now, as has been requested by certain members


of the opposition, to accept sterling to counteract our unbalance of trade with the United Kingdom.
I do not think we should use anything like three or four hundred millions of dollars to prime an already dry socialist well. I shall not take the time to trace developments in the organization of the union at Kimberley, except to say that through tireless efforts the union has reached the stage where it commands the respect of the community and the company, and at present operates under the best collective bargaining agreement in Canada.
Prior to organization the work week was fifty-six hours, with no consideration for statutory holidays; and, in general, conditions were such as would be found in any unorganized camp-with the exception of the fact that living conditions had necessarily improved because of permanency in employment. I neglected to say earlier that the developed ore body, at the present rate of reduction, will last for another fifty years. That has been known for a long time, and with that in mind employees invested and built their own homes.
The Sullivan mine is the first and only hard-rock mine in Canada working on a forty-hour week basis. By adopting the forty-hour week twenty per cent more people were put on the payroll and given employment. Since that time production has gone up to the extent of 2,000 tons a day because of the new methods of extraction and haulage introduced by the company. Working on the forty-hour week they are producing 2,000 tons more than were being produced before the introduction of the union agreement.
I shall run through quickly some of the other features in this agreement. There is an excellent seniority system. This system gives seniority to veterans returning from the services, regardless of whether they have had previous service with the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, the operators of this mine. They may return after one to six years of service in the armed forces, enter the employ of the company, and, after ninety days, will be credited with six years' seniority rights.
We have a labour-management committee which works in an advisory capacity, a joint safety committee, which has done excellent work. I am happy to say that the Sullivan mine came very close to winning the award for its safety record in the last year. We have a contract committee, and the miners are working on a contract basis. The contract committee have been able to maintain contract prices at a rate sufficiently high that

some miners last year had earnings which exceeded considerably the indemnity paid to members of parliament.
We have a good arbitration procedure for the settlement of disputes. We receive overtime pay for all work performed in excess of eight hours. We receive pay for statutory holidays when not worked, and double time if worked; two weeks vacation with pay; and we have the check-off of union dues. Last, but not least, we have wage rates ranging from $1.09 plus a shift differential of four and eight cents to $1.53 per hour for safety miners. In addition each employee customarily receives $75 as a Christmas bonus. Also a non-contributory pension plan which, at the present rate of pay for a miner with a lifetime of service, would amount to between $90 and $100 per month.
In connection with sick benefits the Kimberley employees have a sick benefit society. This was not brought into effect entirely by the union, but has been improved upon immensely. To this society we pay $1.50 a month, which amount is matched by the company under a recent bargaining agreement. In this way $1.50 is paid by the employee and $1.50 by the company. The directors have the right to change the figure that will be paid in benefits'. But, at least for the present, I understand that for the first month a member if off sick will receive $4 a day for thirty days, increasing to $5, and for the last one hundred days of the year he will receive $6 a day or $180 a month.
We have a medical set-up. The fee is $3.50, and includes everything-doctor, hospital, specialists' fees, and travelling by railway, T.C.A. or C.P.A. We hire C.P.A. if it is necessary to take an employee to a specialist-and at no additional cost to the member. By agreement the company matches this payment. I have not the time to go into them in detail, but an employee need have no worry as regards medical expenses or hospitalization so long as he is a member of the society. He might be in hospital for some years, but through all that time he would be attended by a doctor and would be given full coverage so long as dues payments were met.
