Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment to the amendment particularly because the first clause deals with agricultural markets and suggestions for their recapture. I am going to 'speak also about the fruit industry. I realize that a number of hon. members have already touched on this matter but I make no apology because I represent a riding in which are grown 75 per cent of all the apples grown in British Columbia. I feel also that I have some experience in this regard because at one time I was a fruit grower and have been in close contact with the fruit industry for thirty years. My home town of Kelowna is right in the centre of the fruit growing district.
I should like to deal briefly with the chaotic condition which existed in that industry thirty years ago. At that time there was no organization and the fruit was sold where it could be sold at any price at all. Various firms, unorganized in many cases, would get the fruit on consignment and then proceed to dump it on any market at any price that would give them any profit. Such was the condition in the early days that the fruit growers became so desperate that they organized one of the finest organizations in Canada, the tree fruit board.
At the present time all our fruit is properly handled, packed and graded for shipment all over the world. We are proud of the tree fruit board. We had difficulties to overcome because, taking just one item, we are 4,000 miles farther away from Great Britain than Nova Scotia. In order to overcome this handicap the quality of the product was improved, as well as the quality of the pack. The result is that today the tree fruit board handles roughly $25 million worth of fruit products grown in the interior of British Columbia.
It should be noted that a good deal of our fruit is sold to the United States, which brings United States dollars to Canada. A current review of agricultural conditions in
392	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Jones Canada states that during 1947-48 and 194849 the United States purchased 1,500,000 bushels and 2,150,000 bushels respectively of Canadian apples, and in both years over 90 per cent came from British Columbia. In 1948 the apple crop in the United States was smaller than normal and there was a strong demand from that country. I merely point that out to indicate how the exportation of fruit to the United States has brought several millions of dollars to this dominion.
The people engaged in the growing of fruit are very cosmopolitan. Practically every race on earth is engaged in fruit growing.
I often think that it would be beneficial if the United Nations could come into our valley to see how these people live so happily togeth'er. Even the odd Russian fruit grower gets along quite well with his Japanese and Anglo-Saxon friends. They all have something in common, the welfare of the industry in which they are engaged.
There are from 120,000 to 150,000 people living in our valley which is about 150 miles long and quite narrow in places. I am not going to dwell too much on our climate because I think the press has publicized it sufficiently for the present. While we have had some cold weather, they have also had similar weather in California, so I am offering no apology. However, damage may be quite considerable from frost. It is expected that many of the young trees will have been killed, and considerable damage is expected to have been done to our peach and apricot trees. It is a little early to know the exact damage, but definitely a good deal of damage will be done.
The difficulties faced by these people are numerous. One difficulty is the obtaining of a staple market when you have crop variations. As is known, a tree grows a good crop one year and a poor crop the next, and so on. Scientific efforts have been made to overcome this through controlled deblossoming. We have had to overcome practically every pest known to the orthodox fruit grower, but one of the worst, the coddling moth, has been practically eliminated by the use of D.D.T. and other sprays.
Hail has taken its toll of our crops because that is one thing that cannot be controlled. This year the growers have organized their own insurance company to take care of hail damage. Each grower will be assessed to build up a fund to take care of the odd orchard that is hailed out. Then we also have high winds which sometimes occur when the fruit has matured. If the fruit is not picked in a matter of days, it is lost. Another difficulty is that our crop seasons coincide CMr. Jones.]

with those of Washington and other states. I have tried to outline briefly some of the difficulties with which the fruit growing industry is faced.
In order to overcome some of these difficulties the industry was encouraged by the present government to try to capture the British market. In order to do that they had to grow a different type of apple from the one sold on the Canadian market. The trees had to be pruned in a different way in order to produce the type of apple wanted in the old country. The industry was geared up to produce roughly three to four million boxes of that type of apple. Now that that market has gone it is found that some of the apples being produced are not suitable for the Canadian or United States market.
The normal shipment of that type of apple to Great Britain was from 2,500,000 to 3,500,000 per year. This year all we have sold to Great Britain is 434,000 boxes. Those were purchased by the British food ministry, the Canadian government paying half the cost. We could not market our production this year and at least a million and a half boxes would be wasted. The growers took the bull by the horns and decided they were not going to have that waste. Without waiting for any arrangement to be made by the government or by any other body they decided hastily

the product is perishable and must be taken care of quickly-to send 1,150,000 boxes to Great Britain as a gift. The alternative was waste and, later on, dumping.
In addition we sell 500,000 boxes to the fruit juice processors at anything from $7 to $9 per ton, or an average of $8. Incidentally this price does not cover the cost of production.
The cost of production is made up quite simply. First there is the cost of packing. Most of those apples were already packed and had borne the packing costs. The cost of handling, packing and storing a box of apples runs from 90 cents to $1; and that charge is usually against the apples in storage. The cost of growing apples varies according to the size of the operation, the type of land, the location of land-whether it faces north, south, east or west-and the size and quality of the crop; but roughly speaking the cost varies from 75 cents to $1.25, or an average of $1. I am referring now to bare costs; I am not including any profit or anything else.
This year we had to handle over eight million boxes; and it has been a problem. Naturally the farmers are reluctant to seek assistance from the government. I feel that they are being a little modest, however, because during the war they accepted ceiling

prices on apples, but for which they would have made much greater profits and been able to build up reserves to take care of a situation such as that with which they are faced this year. Then there is the high taxation on fruit land, especially for provincial purposes; irrigation is costly, and there are many other expenses. I realize that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is fully aware of these conditions; and though we have heard a good deal of criticism of his actiorfs in other matters, I will say that he has given considerable assistance to the fruit growers of the Okanagan valley and British Columbia generally.
One of the greatest things to happen was the culmination of our fight, which extended over a period of thirteen years, for a marketing act. As hon. members know, last year that marketing act was passed and is now in operation. But these things in themselves are not sufficient to overcome the difficulties now facing the growers. We have conditions that are beyond their control, especially the dollar shortage and the loss of the United Kingdom market. I need not go into the history of that, because hon. members know it as well as I do. It is principally because of the loss of this market, and the fact that in order to avoid waste we had to send a gift of 1,150,000 boxes of apples overseas, that I appeal to the government to consider the emergency that has arisen this year.
The government have wisely set aside $200 million placed at the disposal of the board for the support of agricultural prices. That legislation states that it is intended to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations. I would point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that under no circumstances can the fruit growers, with the present market, having in mind the deficiencies I have mentioned, obtain enough revenue to give them a fair return; so now the time has come when they require this assistance. I know the difficulty, and I fully believe it is temporary. On that basis I am making my appeal.
Any assistance given should be at least to the extent of the cost of production and the cost of handling already incurred by the growers. I have given that figure roughly as $2. I should like also to see the grower given a reasonable profit, to enable him to maintain a decent standard of living. I am not asking this for a bunch of people who are doing nothing to help themselves. The fruit growers have done a great deal. They have increased production; they have improved their grading and packing; they have done everything possible through cold storage to extend their season. They have set aside 55946-26
The Address-Mr. Jones a large sum of money for advertising, and are now working on the theory that the Canadian market itself can be improved. I believe it can. In 1948 the per capita consumption of apples in Canada was 33 pounds. In 1949 it fell to 27 pounds. I believe we can not only recapture lost ground abroad but also improve Canadian consumption, because after all 27 pounds of apples per person per year is not a large quantity. They have also tried to improve the quality of their apples by assistance from the dominion experimental farm at Summerland. This year they are making a grant of $5,000 to that farm for special work on pests and other problems with which they are still faced.
So I believe these producers have done everything possible to retain their export market; but, as I pointed out, matters of international trade and world conditions are definitely beyond their control. Fruit is unlike any other crop. As the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) pointed out, trees are at their prime for from twelve to thirty years. During that period of productivity many changes may take place; wars, depressions, loss of markets and so on. The fruit grower is stuck; he must carry on. His trees are there, whether he likes it or not, for that period of years; and he must take the ups and downs of our economic system in his stride. The grower must be assisted to carry on, because he becomes either a permanent asset or a permanent liability; and an asset is far better than a liability. In prosperous years he is a heavy taxpayer. He pays high taxes on his land, high income taxes, and high irrigation taxes. He is an employer of labour on a large scale; and he maintains himself and his family on a fairly high standard of living. During the odd year like this he needs help to tide him over until once more he has access to his old markets.
I refer once more to the legislation under which I am making this appeal. It states that the board is to endeavour to insure adequate and stable returns for agricultural products. That statement covers my request. Some $200 million has been set aside annually, and the unexpended portion goes back into the general revenue. They have the power; they have the money; but I believe any action must be taken before the end of this month. I appeal on behalf of the fruit growers because, being three thousand miles away, they may not have the opportunity to come before the house, at least not en masse. So I ask that assistance be given at least to the extent of the cost of production.
I should like to deal with one other matter in behalf of the municipalities of British Columbia. I do so because I was surprised

The Address-Mr. Jones and alarmed to hear the statement from the other side of the house within the last day or two that the municipalities will be expected to bear a greater share of the cost of unemployment relief. When you say a municipality must bear a greater share of the cost of relief it means that land taxes within that area must be made even higher in order to carry the additional burden. Any further tax on the land within the municipalities of this dominion, particularly in my province, would just about break them. If a depression came along, as it well might, we would see acres of land revert to the municipalities for non-payment of taxes. The growers, to whom I have just referred, would also find themselves in the same unfortunate situation they experienced in the thirties, when they could not raise enough money on their land to pay their taxes.
If this situation arose, there would be insufficient funds to keep any municipality functioning properly. When this situation arose before, it forced many municipalities into the hands of the receiver. I am going to suggest one or two logical methods by which the government could help. One of these methods concerns dominion properties located in municipalities. Last year a bill was passed granting token payments to certain municipalities, on the basis of the amount of dominion property located within that municipality. By and large, this method does not bring any revenue to the smaller towns of our province, because few of them qualify. I believe the government has a responsibility in this regard. Usually a government building, whether it is a post office or a customs building, occupies one of the choicest spots in the municipality, and one which would pay the highest taxes if it were taxable. I know the argument is that the post office renders a service and, therefore, should not be called upon to pay taxes. Liquor stores also render a service, but they are taxable. Revenue producing offices, such as the post office and customs offices, are in a position to at least pay the service charges to the city for road and sidewalk maintenance, police and fire protection; all the services rendered by a city to its inhabitants.
The other method by which the government could help would be by contributing towards the cost of education. In my province, and I assume the same is true of all provinces, the cost of education is increasing rapidly. In many municipalities it now represents 50 per cent of the levied taxes, not only in municipalities but in unorganized territories as well. Building costs and teachers' salaries are both up. I do not believe education should be curbed for lack of money, because through

it we are building citizens for the future. I believe, therefore, that the dominion should enter the field, and the cost of education should be borne by other means than a tax on land. The method of the grant can be controversial, but I am not suggesting any particular method. I merely suggest that such a grant must be made to give some relief to the land taxpayers of our province. A good education naturally makes good Canadians. I believe that any grant the government cares to make should be earmarked for the use of the municipality, or for the reduction of taxes now levied on land.
I have had a great deal to do with this particular question because, like the member for New Westminster, I was in municipal politics before I entered this sphere of activity. I was the mayor of my town for four years, and an alderman for ten years. I was elected with the New Westminster hon. member to the executive of the union of B.C. municipalities, and I was president of that organization for a term. I happened to be chairman of the committee which prepared projects to take care of post-war unemployment. We did that work on the assumption that federal aid would be given to us to carry out those projects. Every municipality in our province co-operated, and we had a fine list of necessary public works ready on the shelf, in case this present situation in Vancouver arose. Without federal aid for our schemes, however, we are absolutely lost. We cannot carry them out. Many of those schemes have now become a must. Practically all of them were self-liquidating projects. For that reason, I am asking the government to again open access to cheap money under the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act, under which money was available at two per cent. I have several requests from municipalities desiring to borrow money under that act, notably Armstrong and En-derby, where the waterworks need renewing. These municipalities hesitate to borrow on the open market at a high rate of interest, but they could handle the low-interest loans available under that act, because they are extended over a reasonable period and are generally self-liquidating.
Another way by which the government could assist the municipalities would be to become realistic about the hospital grant. I realize that, according to the act, the hospital grant was given on the basis of one-third of the total cost, but was not to exceed $1,000 per bed. The cost of building hospitals, however, today is between $6,000 and $7,500 per bed. As a matter of fact a projected modem hospital in Vancouver, it is estimated, will cost $10,500 per bed. I am going to suggest

to the minister that he should at least consider doubling this sum of money to make it more nearly comparable to the higher cost of building today. If one refers to the estimates of last year and the public accounts of this year, one finds that the province of British Columbia estimated it would use $13 million for hospital construction. Actually, only $2,223,000 was used. The reason the province used only 17 per cent of that money is fairly obvious. After the small grant from the dominion government, plus an equal amount from the provincial government, the balance was so great that the hospital boards and municipalities could not handle it. We need the extensions to our hospitals, because of the growth of our population. The institution of the health act in the province of British Columbia has also brought more customers, so to speak, to our hospitals. Every hospital in our province is filled to capacity, and many of them have patients in the corridors awaiting a room. Sometimes patients who are in the hospital for a serious illness are rushed out in order to make room for the next patient.
In conclusion, I might point out to the government that the health and education of our people is a national obligation. I say it is national because I do not believe small units give the best results. I do not believe health should be administered by a small town, in which a part-time doctor is responsible for the health and welfare of the people. It should be put on a broader basis than that. Education should not be carried on as it is today, with one teacher being responsible for four or five different grades. Generally, small units are not very efficient, and it is for that reason the dominion government should enter the field to bring order out of a certain amount of chaos. We need more hospitals; we need more clinics; we need more schools; and only the government can give them. Only this government can afford to be generous. I feel that this government can afford to be particularly generous with the province of British Columbia because a few years ago it made a splendid deal in connection with the tax agreement. In 1948-49, under these agreements, the dominion government collected $148,563,000 in our province, and in return paid $21,960,000.
The income tax is a fair tax. It is based on ability to pay. Evidently my province has the ability to pay approximately $150 million. But I do feel that, in order to keep that province supplied with schools, hospitals and clinics, a bigger proportion of that money should be returned, either by a new agreement or by a more generous grant to the municipalities, in order to meet the increased cost of hospitalization and education.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to avail myself of my privilege to speak in this debate in order to urge the government of my country to grant Count Jacques de Bernonville asylum and the right to remain permanently in Canada.
Convinced of his innocence and of his respectability, I believe it my duty, notwithstanding the difficulties which my attitude may bring upon me, to rise in this house in order to plead for a French citizen who is being persecuted by his political enemies, by French communist organizations and here, in this country, by notorious communist sympathizers.
A shameful campaign of lies and false accusations has been launched, without any proof whatsoever, against this man. I shall endeavour to remove, on the strength of the evidence which I shall produce, the prejudices of which he has been the victim, and to rehabilitate him in the mind of certain hon. members of this house and in the opinion of the public.
Who is this man who for almost four years has been hounded by French communists and Canadian communist sympathizers?
Since the age of 17 and during two world wars, Count Jacques Duge de Bernonville has served his country and the allies.
During the war of 1914-1918 he fought in the French army and won promotions and decorations for gallantry and feats of arms.
He was promoted to officer of the Legion of Honour-the youngest soldier so decorated-he was awarded the Croix de Guerre in 1918 and 1940, mentioned eight times in dispatches, wounded five times; he bears the scars of thirty bullet or shrapnel wounds.
In the interval between both world wars, he held honourable and important posts in industry and business. At the outbreak of hostilities, in 1939, he was appointed commanding officer of a mountain rifle battalion. He fought in the French army and was mentioned once more in dispatches for gallantry. After the armistice, he remained in the French army until demobilization. Arrested by the Germans, he was freed by the advancing allies.
His record of service is such that no one can teach him anything when it comes to patriotism.

The Address-Mr. Arsenault In June, 1944, Jacques de Bernonville was appointed, by order of the government of Marshal Petain, commanding officer of the forces in charge of maintaining order in the military district of Lyons, France.
The following letters are forceful evidence of his record of service during the time he held that post, from June to August, 1944.
Dr. Pierre Bertrand, professor at the Faculty of Medicine, hospital surgeon and mayor of the city of Lyons in 1944, during Herriot's internment, certified as follows on the 22nd of August, 1944:
I met Major Jacques de Bernonville during his stay in Lyons from June, 1944, to the end of August, 1944. He was commanding officer of uniformed troops detailed to maintain order, that is the Mobile Guard, the police and the mobile reserve groups. He was never in charge of militia.
Major de Bernonville's reputation as a fearless and blameless officer preceded him in Lyons. It is with courage and unselfishness that he served, not political ends but his country. During those three months, he performed a difficult task and never issued an order that could have resulted in an attack upon the life of a compatriot or ally or upon the private property of anyone.
Major de Bernonville is entitled to my esteem and to my respect.
(Signed) Pierre Bertrand, Former Mayor of the City of Lyons
(1944)
The following declaration was made at Cap d'Ail on August 27, 1949:
I, the undersigned, Abbe Victor Bouillon, do. on my honour, declare that Major Jacques de Bernonville, to my knowledge, has always behaved as a leader, a good Christian and a gentleman. Far from attacking French citizens or allied soldiers or from interfering with property, he has, during the troubled times from 1940 to 1944, by his courageous attitude towards the Germans and, with the help of the troops which he commanded, ensured the supply of food, protected the people and maintained order, and thus facilitated the task of the allies who, in their advance, found a maximum of order.
I certify that I have myself seen Major de Bernonville at work in 1940, at Cap d'Ail, where he was my faithful and unanimously respected parishioner, and in 1944, at Lyons, where he commanded the troops of the Ministry of Public Order and where I had the honour of being his guest on two occasions. The first time was the 31st of July, on the occasion of a sermon which he had asked me to give during a mass organized by him, with the consent of His Eminence Cardinal Gerlier, for all the forces detailed to maintain order and which took place the next day, July 22, in St. Bonaventure church. The second time was three weeks later, on the 14th of August, when, passing through Lyons I had supper and spent the night at his home.
On the 15th, he personally served my mass and together with several of his officers received Holy Communion. Everything I have known or heard about him at that time, the universal respect in which he was held-his officers and men worshipped him-even the atmosphere of his home, force me to state that I believe that he filled a difficult

mission with a self-denial, a devotion to duty and a perfect honesty which would, in normal circumstances have brought him the gratitude of the nation instead of the persecution he now suffers.
In witness thereof, I freely certify the above and, in order to re-establish the truth, without any intention of interfering in a case which comes under the jurisdiction of the Canadian government, I declare, as a priest and as a Frenchman, that Canada would have everything to gain in allowing a man like Major de Bernonville. a great fighter, a true Christian and patriot, to settle among people who are known for their generosity and their chivalry.
(Signed) Father V. Bouillon,
Doctor in Theology,
Laureate of the French Academy, Former parish priest at Cap d'Ail, Missionary in the diocese of Nice.
Here is a further declaration, by an officer of the Legion of Honour:
I, the undersigned, Colonel Groussard, certify that I met Mr. Jacques de Bernonville during the year 1940. Monsieur de Bernonville struck me as being an absolutely straightforward and honest person, incapable of meanness, and I am sure that he never, in any way, went counter to his principles as a good Christian.
Paris, October 30, 1948 (Signed) G. Groussard

Mr. Speaker, the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne is of great value in one particular respect. Coming at the beginning of the session, it enables hon. members to explain the thoughts and hopes of the people they represent much better than can be done as the session runs on. While the period between the last session of this house and the present session was very short, we did have an opportunity to meet our constituents. That was so even in Vancouver, in spite of the deep snow about which I have heard so much from eastern members since my return. By way of standing up for my own city may I remind Your Honour and hon. members that today the people of Vancouver will be looking at their snowdrops and crocuses while back here it is fifteen below zero, with a north wind. So the west coast is still the banana belt of Canada.
During that intervening period there have been many far-reaching developments. For example, we have had the disclosure, with


all it implies to the future of mankind, that hydrogen bombs can be made. We have seen the continuation of the spread of communism in Asia. Many disturbing things have happened, and I believe our people are deeply worried over the situation throughout the world. There has been a great deal of disillusionment in the minds of all thinking people; and that is easily understood. This is a time of great uncertainty for thinking Canadians; and that being so a strong lead from parliament would be most helpful.
This evening I have four suggestions to offer as to what parliament could do at this session to give a lead to the Canadian people. The first is that we keep Canada standing firmly with the other peoples of the world who want peace, yet who are unafraid and are prepared to beat down any aggression. This brings to mind those young Canadians serving in our forces, both active and reserve. I believe we have a splendid group of young men serving Canada. They must be enabled to maintain efficiency and, perhaps even more important, must be made to feel that their efforts are appreciated by their fellow Canadians.
Hon. members will recall that within the last few days some of those young men have been taking part in a military exercise known as Exercise Sweetbriar. It is significant that the area in which that operation was held was the Yukon and Alaska. We must be realistic about the situation today. The shortest and easiest route to the arsenals of democracy and in fact to the heart of democracy is across Bering strait to Alaska, into northern Canada and so on to the United States. The Soviet now has standing with her the communist regime in China, a nation of over four hundred million people. I hope there will be no trouble, but Russia plus China adds up to Canada being probably in greater danger under present conditions than any other democratic nation in the world.
If serious trouble should come in the Pacific area it will probably be in the north rather than the south Pacific. So I warn this parliament that it behooves Canada to take the lead in bringing the nations of the Pacific together, rather than assuming the role of an observer in Pacific affairs. I was disturbed by the attitude displayed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) in his address the other day. Mind you, it was gratifying to have him emphasize the importance of the Pacific area; but in reporting on the conference so recently held at Colombo he seemed to take the attitude that Canada was just sitting in. For example, he used this expression: "Canada was a dollar

country at a sterling party." I know that in using those words he was referring particularly to currency problems, but that indicated his attitude. Again he said, "Canada was a persistent dollar gadfly." Then with respect to the commonwealth consultative committee, the formation of which was recommended by that conference, he made no statement as to whether or not Canada would join; in fact he said it would be of meagre value unless the United States also joined. I was reminded of the attitude taken a year or two ago when we had to have our ambassador at Washington assure the state department there that at a conference to be held at Canberra nothing would be decided. In effect the minister damned with faint praise this suggestion of a commonwealth consultative committee; and that attitude is not in line with the menace to Canada in the Pacific area. I hope that when the minister speaks tomorrow he will tell us that Canada has decided to join that committee, and I further hope he will say that the Canadian government has decided to advocate a Pacific pact just as there is a North Atlantic pact.
I believe we would have support for such a proposal. I have here a dispatch from Bangkok, Thailand, dated February 15 and headed, "U.S. diplomats want Pacific alliance." There is a great demand for a Pacific pact; and under present conditions Canada's position is so dangerous that she should take the lead in advocating such a pact. At the present time we are in the ridiculous position that of all the nations of the commonwealth only Great Britain and Canada are in the North Atlantic pact. Australia, New Zealand and South Africa cannot join.
My second suggestion as to what this parliament could do by way of giving a lead to the Canadian people at this time is that we could enact legislation at this session to raise the standard of living of those Canadians who are in want. That is extremely important when we are faced with the menace of communism. Our failure to take steps of this kind is our Achilles heel when we are attacked by Canadian communists within our own country.
Let me give you some examples of what we could do. First of all, today no one accepts any responsibility for the employable unemployed, unless they are qualified for unemployment insurance. There are many thousands who cannot qualify for that insurance. The belief is held across the country that the care of these men and women is the responsibility of the dominion government. This government should say what responsibility it will accept for those people who are having such a difficult time. I am afraid the government is evading that ques-
The Address-Mr. Green tion. I hope a statement will be made during this session as to just what responsibility Ottawa will accept.
Another example would be the raising of the ceiling on permissible income under the Old Age Pensions Act, to correspond with the increase in pension which was provided about a year ago. Because that was not done, at least a quarter of the old age pensioners in Canada did not get the full benefit of that increase. I believe the figure is approximately 63,000 senior citizens of Canada. This means that we penalized thrift, because those people who did not get the full benefit of the increase were the people who had some small income.
I suggest further that we should, at this session, establish a system of contributory pensions and abolish the means test. The vast majority of Canadians are willing to pay towards a contributory pension scheme. They have no other way of saving enough to retire when they reach an advanced age. I venture to say that few of the members of this house have any other way of providing for their old age, taxation and the cost of living being so high today. By and large, the Canadian people are in that position. We should no longer delay in making it possible for them to protect themselves under a contributory pension scheme.
Then, too, I believe there are few Canadians who do not wish to have the means test abolished. They resent the humiliation of that means test. It is un-Canadian, and it should go. It is going to go; it is just a matter of time before it is a thing of the past. It is delaying adequate industrial pensions in Canada. I believe most of the members of this house, when they stood for election, promised the electors that they would abolish the means test. Yet, in the second session of this parliament, it is quite obvious there is no intention of removing that means test. All we are to get is a committee, which is to review the whole question and then report at the end of the session. You know, Mr. Speaker, I know, and everybody in the house knows, that is merely a delaying action.
Another group who are in want, and who should be helped at this session, are the older veterans of Canada, the men who served this nation on the battlefields of France and Belgium. In the speech from the throne, there is a statement that the war veterans' allowance is to be made payable to those veterans who served in the allied forces. The government is to be congratulated on taking that step, even though it only comes after some of us have been advocating it for 15 years. I hope the legislation will be wide

The Address-Mr. Green enough to cover the men who served in the South African war, as well as those who served in the first great war.
Other amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act are urgently required. I believe the war veterans' allowance should be increased to equal the old age pension. In British Columbia the old age pensioner draws $50 per month and his wife draws $50 per month, making a total of $100. In addition, both man and wife get free hospitalization, dental care and other benefits. On the other hand, the recipient of the war veterans' allowance, the man who served this country in the trenches, receives only about $40 if single, and about $70 if married. He may get hospitalization, but his wife does not. As a matter of fact, under the provincial hospitalization scheme, the veteran is compelled to pay a certain amount to the provincial government to cover his wife's hospitalization. It can only come out of his small veterans' allowance. I know of one case where a man who served in the German forces during the first great war came out here and settled, and he and his wife are now drawing an old age pension of $100. The Canadian veteran who served against him can only get approximately $70. That is a ridiculous situation, and it should be remedied at this session.
Furthermore, the time has come to decentralize the administration of the War Veterans Allowance Act. First-class administrators are now available in the districts, as well as adequate staffs. They are in close contact with the veteran, and able to deal with his case without delay. The war veterans' allowance board in Ottawa are out of touch with the veteran. Mind you, this board have done a great deal of good work, but they simply cannot appreciate the position of the veteran in the same way as the men who are out there living with him. There are long delays. I believe it sometimes takes as long to get a decision from the board in Ottawa as it took to investigate the case out in the province. Furthermore, if there are overpayments, it means delay in getting the matter adjusted. The first thing the veteran knows, he receives a letter telling him he has to pay back a large sum of money. I believe if these applications for war veterans' allowance were dealt with locally, with an appeal to the board in Ottawa, there would be far more satisfaction and far more fairness, as well as quicker action in dealing with these cases. Remember, when a man needs the war veterans' allowance, he needs jt in a hurry. He is not in a position to wait for a long time for a decision from Ottawa.
I intended to say something about the men in the merchant navy, but the members of the

house know my position on that question quite well. They should be getting far better treatment than they have received. I hope something will be done for them at this session.
Also, I endorse the appeals made by so many members of the house in this debate, that a special committee on veterans affairs should be set up at this session, the second session of this parliament; and there has been no such committee yet. There are many new members in this parliament. They should be given the opportunity of becoming acquainted with veterans legislation; and the rest of us should be given the benefit of their views as to what should be done to improve that legislation.
My third suggestion has to do with improving the efficiency of the government, and I am looking right at the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier). In these days of threats of war and mounting unemployment, with the cost of living at an all-time high and with taxation still at wartime levels, the Canadian people become exasperated when they learn that the government is not observing businesslike precautions in awarding contracts, and is awarding those contracts to favourites. This has happened recently in Vancouver with regard to at least three public buildings, namely the Alvin building, the Begg building and the Catelli building.
There was some discussion about two of those buildings on the last day of the last session. If hon. members wish to refer to that discussion they will find it at page 3112 of Hansard of 1949. After the session ended the Minister of Public Works was good enough to send me the documents which I had requested when asking him questions on that last day.
Let us take the first one, the Alvin building. On April 6, 1948, an order in council was passed authorizing the Minister of Public Works to enter into a lease of a building to be constructed. I have here the order in council. It set out that there was a shortage of office accommodation in Vancouver and that was true, but there were buildings which could have been purchased, I believe. The order in council reads:
An offer has been obtained, however, from the Alvin Estates Limited to construct a fireproof building on their property-
I direct attention to those words "on their property".
__and to rent it to the crown on the following terms
and conditions.
It was to be a four-storey and basement fireproof building and the rental was to be $96,000 a year, which is quite a substantial

rental. The period of the lease was to be ten years from the date of occupation, and the government was to get an option to purchase the property at $554,000 at any time within the first twelve months of occupation.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, that the order in council sets out that the lease is to be from Alvin Estates Limited. No tenders at all were called. There was no competition. The company was not in existence at the time, I believe; it was incorporated a week or so later, on April 14, 1948. At all material times there have been three shareholders, and the same persons have been directors. There may have been the odd qualifying director, but substantially there were three shareholders and three directors. Two of them, Messrs. Allan and Viner, of the contracting firm of Allan and Viner Construction Company Limited, and the third, Mr. Braidwood, solicitor, all three close to the government. They apparently found out that there was a chance to do business with the government. The Minister of Public Works, in his answers to be found at page 3112 of last year's Hansard, told me that in March of 1948-and that is the month before the order in council-Alvin Estates Limited offered to construct a four-storey building. As I say, the company apparently was not incorporated until after the order in council was passed. It did not acquire the property until June 11, 1948, when such property was obtained from those same three men for $45,000. One-third of the property had been held for a couple of years by one of the men and the other two-thirds had been acquired by the others in May, 1948, for $7,000 each. That is, those two men apparently paid $14,000.
Then on July 20, 1948, another order in council was passed. This means that it is not a matter for the Minister of Public Works only. Each step was taken by the cabinet. I have here the order in council for July 20, 1948. It sets out that there shall be three more storeys put on the building and the figures go up to a yearly rental of $146,940, with a purchase price of $862,155. The order in council also sets out that there had been a parliamentary vote, number 828, for $800,000 for purchase, alterations and extensions from Alvin Estates Limited. Here again no tenders were called and there was no competition. I think it is reasonable to assume that these three men were able to finance their construction largely on the basis of the fact that they had a government lease. Debentures were issued. Although I cannot verify this, I am told that most of those debentures were held by the three men, doubtless being put up with the bank or some other lending institution as security for their financing.

The figures now go up by $200,950, until the annual rental mentioned in this order in council is $183,995; and mind you, this is for a ten-year lease which means getting as rent over $1,800,000 and having the building after that. The total purchase price, if the option is exercised, has now gone up to $1,063,105. The order in council sets out that it is the intention to exercise the option to purchase the building within the time specified, and goes on to say that the rental is so high that the option should be exercised quickly. This was over a year ago. The copy I have shows that the monthly rental is $13,332.90 but I think that is a mistake and the figure should be $15,332.90. The order in council, in its last paragraph, gives authority to go ahead and complete the purchase.
When I questioned the Minister of Public Works in December he said that his department was going to exercise the option and buy the building. Then there was a good deal of publicity in Vancouver, and I understand the option has not yet been exercised. The government is still paying this rent of $15,332.90 a month and apparently only a few days remain within which the government can exercise the option. I am told the date is March 16.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that this business was handed out by the government to favourites. No tenders were called. No attempt was made to call tenders. The city assessment of the property is $508,725. The building permit for which application was made was about $451,000 although I believe that was meant to cover only the original arrangement. The contractors did not bother to take out any further building permits. If this deal is carried through the total cost to the country will be $1,063,105, plus whatever rental has been paid, which I think will amount to between $100,000 and $200,000 additional.
In Vancouver this deal is the talk of the town. It is considered fantastic by the man in the street, by responsible construction men, by real estate men and by the workmen who worked on the building. The Vancouver Sun, which is an ardent supporter of this government-

I say to the minister and to the government that we look to the government, and we look to our own British Columbia minister, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew), to see that this mess is cleaned up, and cleaned up quickly.
The second building, the Begg building, was authorized to be purchased by order in council on April 20, 1948, for $375,000. It was an automobile sales building, and that price was plenty. On January 7, 1949, a contract for extension was let to Allan and Viner Construction Company, Limited. All this took place at the time they were building the Alvin building. The contract was for $850,000. There was no competition; there were no tenders. The contract says they are to get a fee of $25,000. I believe it is the custom on the coast also to have sub-trades allow a certain commission, in some instances as high as 10 per cent. On August 24, 1949, the cabinet increased that figure by $200,000 to $1,050,000. On that increase of $200,000 the firm is allowed an additional 3 per cent. Since then I believe it has gone up another $375,000, so that the repairs and improvements to that building are costing $1,425,000, making with the original purchase price a total of $1,850,000, and I believe the work is not yet completed. It was not completed when I left Vancouver.
The third building is the Catelli building. The contract to change over that building was given to the same firm during the same period without any tenders, without any competition, at a figure of $67,197. That makes a total over $2,500,000, without any tenders, given to the same group. The government has no right to use public funds in this way. The government has no right to allow anyone to have the inside track. Therefore I suggest that at this session parliament could and should act to improve the efficiency of government in Canada.
My fourth suggestion as to what this parliament could do by way of giving a lead to the Canadian people is that it could enact legislation to ensure that Canadians are enabled to carry on with the building of a great nation by providing that our Canadian resources will be used in Canada to the maximum extent possible rather than being sold out to the United States. That is particularly important now with our promising discoveries of oil, natural gas, iron and uranium. These resources can be the pillars upon which we build a great nation. They are essential for greatness in the second half of the twentieth century. Canada needs a national oil and gas policy. We also need a


national iron and steel policy both designed to give the Canadian people the utmost benefit from these resources. Without such a policy much of the benefit will go to the people of the United States. By and large they are the people who are putting up the money for these developments and naturally enough if the Canadian government, if the Canadian parliament, does not adopt a national policy the people of the United States will get just as large a proportion of these natural resources as they possibly can.
I believe-and I am glad the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) got back today, and is here-that the government's policy is to sell as large quantities as possible of these raw natural resources to the United States, namely, oil, gas and iron. We know that the government is sending our oil down to Superior, Wisconsin. With regard to natural gas, last year we had the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) battling to force through a bill for a company that was going to pipe natural gas down into the states of Washington and Oregon before it got to British Columbia. With iron, members might just wait and see if the policy will not be the same; get it down to Massachusetts, get it down to Cleveland; sell it in the raw state and get the money for it, and do not worry so much about using it here in Canada to the largest extent possible, to build up this nation. Sending these commodities to the United States in that way means jobs in the United States. It means that your son and mine will probably have to migrate to the United States to get work. In the next fifty years it may mean Canada becoming a satellite of the United States rather than, a great nation in her own right.
In respect of these discoveries, these great resources, we are trustees for the Canadians of the future. What this parliament does about them in the next four or five years may well be the deciding factor in Canada's rate of progress in the remainder of this century.
These are my four suggestions, Mr. Speaker. In conclusion may I say I believe that each of these suggestions meets with the hearty approval of the citizens of Vancouver-Quadra, whom I have the honour to represent in this house, regardless of their political allegiance; and I place these suggestions before the government and more particularly before the private members of the house. I have more confidence in them than I have in the members of the cabinet. I place these suggestions before the house for that serious and earnest consideration which I believe is characteristic of the members of this present parliament.

The hon. member is speaking of the site now, not of the building. I am not going to speak of external affairs or any other matter tonight; I am going to refer only to these three questions. I believe the hon. member has spoken in good faith but I am going to try to prove that I was right in following advice. The Public Works Act states that I must follow the advice of these people and I did. That will be my defence in connection with these three deals.
It was said that this was giving things to friends of the government. I do not think my officials know these people, and I certainly do not know them. I have never met them nor seen them. You cannot expect the Minister of Public Works to go all over the country meeting contractors and deciding whether they will be given work. I am advised, and the law says I should be advised by certain people in the department. In the seven years and five months that I have been there I have been well advised.
Coming now to the three deals. In 1947 the pressure for more space in Vancouver was considerable, particularly from three departments. There were nights that I could not sleep thinking that unemployment insurance might be put out on the street when we were thrown out of the Vancouver hotel. At that time income tax occupied six different buildings, the Winch building, post office building, the Metropolitan building, the Macaulay-Nicolls building, the Begg building, and then for storage purposes, the Winch building, the post office, the Royal Insurance

building and the immigration building. That was the income tax set-up in 1947 in Vancouver.
I do not know just how many buildings unemployment insurance occupied. There was no continuity in the government service in the set-up of those departments. How did that come up?
During the war no office building was built in Vancouver. The last building was started in 1933 and completed in 1939. We did get some space at the beginning of the war under rent control and we were so harsh with those people that members of this house who are sitting right here tonight came to ask me to vacate space occupied by the government in order to give young veterans who were coming back from the war a chance to establish themselves in business or the professions. I am looking now at hon. members who came to me to make that request.
In the fall of 1947 I had a report from Mr. Dawson on space that could be rented or bought. During the war and even up to 1947, the policy of the government was not to put up public buildings. We wanted to give the people a chance at the materials and labour available. Some of the largest construction associations in the country sent me resolutions and letters asking that public buildings be not constructed by the federal government because of the great demand for labour and materials. When my estimates were being discussed in the house in 1946 and 1947 I do not know how many members told me that I was right in not having public buildings constructed. During those years my estimates were kept down to about $15 million.
In 1947 the war had been over for two years and the demand for space was still pressing. We could not put up buildings but space had to be found and I, as Minister of Public Works acting as agent for the other departments, had to find space. What did we do? Mr. Dawson is the resident architect in Vancouver. He has lived there nearly all his life except when he was overseas during the war. He was born, bred and educated as an architect in Birmingham, England, and then he spent the rest of his life in Vancouver. The reports I get from Vancouver are that Mr. Dawson is so honest that no one in that province would dare to make any insinuations against him. I have been told so by the highest authorities in the province. He has had the confidence of my department ever since he has been in that district. I have found him to be a good adviser and under the act I am supposed to follow the advice which it is one of his duties to give.
He became so discouraged about the situation that I sent out Mr. Cherry, the head real

Mr. Speaker, the economic problems and the bright prospects in certain parts of both western and eastern Canada have been skilfully outlined by the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I congratulate them on their success and greatly rejoice in the praise that they have received in this house.
In the constituency which I have the great honour of representing here, the main concern of civil and religious authorities at the moment is the struggle against unemployment.
Last September, when I took part in the debate, I warned the government that this evil had appeared in Canada, that the people were looking to the fast approaching winter with anxiety and that it was urgent to take the necessary steps to deal with this calamitous possibility. No suggestion was put forward, however, no steps were taken to check the progress of a trend which is fatal to both the material and moral life of our
412	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Gagnon working classes. People now are troubled and gripped with anxiety. The fear of want has now become a nightmare, and idleness an overwhelming burden.
Days of misfortune are still close at hand and the worker, mindful of the depression of the thirties, has an inner fear of want and of the spectre of misery hovering over himself and his family.
Insecurity is the worker's greatest- enemy.
The federal authorities knew this deeply human feeling when they stated in the speech from the throne, in January, 1944:
The post-war objective of our domestic policy is social security and human welfare.
To have ideals and noble principles, or a set of comprehensive plans hidden in a drawer is one thing. Implementing them, passing from the theoretical and blueprint stage to the carrying-out of the plans is another.
But the Hon. C. D. Howe did say, in 1945, when he was Minister of Reconstruction and Supply:
In the interest of members of the three armed forces and of the civilian population, our reconstruction program should ensure a smooth and orderly transition from economic conditions that prevailed during the war to conditions that are consistent with the return of peace, but such as will maintain a high and stable degree of employment and earnings. That is the first item in the government's program. And when I say that we are aiming at a high and stable degree of employment and income, it means nothing short of full employment. The government know that employment and income will be subject to fluctuations of international trade that cannot be fully or immediately overcome; they also know that seasonal fluctuations resulting from our climate and established trade practices can be overcome only by much patience and skill.
It seems that those two qualities have been lacking in our ministers. In view of such clear and perfectly true statements, the policy of our present leaders is surprising, to say the least.
The authorities do not seem to realize that everything has come about as they had foreseen. Yet they make no concrete proposal to alleviate the people's hardships. Whatever improvements or amendments the Unemployment Insurance Act undergoes, this can only bring temporary relief instead of a permanent solution for this chronic evil.
With respect to employment and earnings, government expenditures fall in three categories.


The minister of reconstruction continued:
First, current expenses for goods and services;
Second, transfer of sums such as pensions, allowances and similar payments;
Third, capital expenditures or public investments for buildings, equipment, roads, airports and other construction or improvement projects of a lasting nature. The last mentioned expenditures can, up to a certain point, be timed to contribute to employment when the need is felt.
The time has come to carry out this program, to help the unemployed, to alleviate the cruel suffering of the low income groups and of the poor.
The government announced in 1945 that it intended to make expenditures likely to provide alternative sources of income in areas affected by the ups and downs of export markets and also to contend with the majority of our economic crises at the very moment they appear rather than after they have spread throughout our whole economic system.
What are we waiting for to translate these fine words into actions? The people of my constituency, who did a wonderful job from the military, industrial and agricultural viewpoints between 1939 and 1945, are particularly affected by the depression that has prevailed for the last six months. For instance, he Soleil, a Liberal newspaper, dealing with the situation in my constituency, wrote on February 10, 1950:
It is not without reason that the Chicoutimi area is applying for public works to assist families affected by unemployment. There are hundreds of them in the erstwhile prosperous centres of Chicoutimi, Arvida and J cnquiere.
On the whole, it can be said that thousands of men, women and children are suffering from hunger. One lives poorly on unemployment insurance, and very miserably when he has to rely on family allowances to buy bread.
It is also the duty of the dominion government to help the working people of the Saguenay district. It can be readily seen that they have had to suffer from conditions that prevailed during the transitional period that followed the war. When the needs of new industries exceeded the number of workers that could be found in that farming region, official agencies urged entire families to move out there. They were not told that work would be of a temporary nature only and that their employment depended on the war which Canada was fighting due to fortuitous circumstances. In several cases, travelling expenses were paid to people who agreed to work in industries essential to the war effort. Under the circumstances, I believe the government should look after those families that are on the verge of starvation due to regional unemployment that could have been foreseen.
They could have been indeed, since, in 1945, the minister of reconstruction stated:
There will be some disorganization and unavoidable delay in a few areas where wartime demands

entailed a large concentration of orders and an abnormal increase in population. In these centres more than elsewhere, cancellation of war contracts will require considerable adjustment.
The government, through the department of reconstruction, is working out plans to settle these local difficulties. They will be carried out to the extent deemed necessary and desirable, special attention being given housing projects and public works.
We ask nothing more, Mr. Speaker.
My constituents have long been asking that level crossings be eliminated, especially in the city of Chicoutimi, where they are very dangerous; that the wharves of Grande Baie and Petit Saguenay be repaired; that public buildings and breakwaters be put up since they are more and more urgently required. Such useful and necessary improvements would not only fill serious gaps but, if undertaken immediately, would help to restore economic stability.
The task of those gentlemen who manage the business of this country is to afford every citizen the opportunity to exercise his right to work, since work is the source of national wealth, happiness and prosperity. It behooves them to carry out this urgent obligation. The sight of all these good people, full of health, energy and courage yet condemned to inaction and idleness, is both painful and heartbreaking.
The state, to whose expenses they have contributed by their taxes and their labour, treats them with less kindness than it does foreigners.
Pariahs are still being recruited in Europe and our country is being flooded with seedy aliens at a time when the homeland has nothing to offer to those who have spent themselves on her behalf. This is both outrageous and absurd.
Immigration is one of the causes of the present unemployment. Any argument to the contrary notwithstanding, the 362,451 immigrants who entered Canada from September 1, 1945 to December 31, 1949, have taken jobs that were occupied or should be occupied by Canadians.
If it is true that today about 375,000 people are out of work, it is because of the mass of refugees which has overrun our shores and crowded the labour market. Our workers are now the victims of this overgenerous policy.
As a matter of fact immigration has never, in this country, shown itself to be the wonderful thing that railway and transportation company propaganda claimed.
The Address-Mr. Gagnon
Every attempt made by Canada to bring in immigrants has ended in failure.
Between 1900 and 1933 we received 4,671,927 immigrants who had come over to settle in Canada. This immigration cost the Canadian taxpayer $80 million. During that time 4,013,523 Canadians emigrated to various parts of the world. Out of 340,000 new arrivals between 1925 and 1927, 282,000 made their way into the United States. If we consider the natural rate of increase we will notice that our population has increased at about the normal rate and that in this connection immigration has played quite a minor role.
Speaking about Canada's experience in this field during the 90-year period from 1851 to 1941, Mr. Herbert Marshall, dominion statistician, stated before the Senate committee in 1946:
Undoubtedly, Canada since 1851 has brought in several million more immigrants than she could absorb. It was a disturbing and costly step but the fact that there was an outlet to the United States prevented the situation from becoming more serious.
He reminded the committee that this outlet is now closed and that therefore:
The present long-term immigration policy of Canada must be as closely related to present needs as possible. If immigrants were admitted as in the past in larger number than we could absorb them, the results would be disastrous.
That statement is clear and definite.
Our workers' minds are filled with gloomy forebodings under the constant threat of lowered standards of living because of the newcomers' willingness to accept any job, at any wages and under any conditions, in order to escape want and starvation.
Immigration must not provide a supply of workers for unscrupulous employers to hire at lower wages in order to increase their profits at the expense of local labour.
Let us remember that during the decade before the first world war, when immigration was flourishing, when vast and choice farm land was available, when huge amounts of capital were flowing into Canada, our capacity of absorption was at its peak.
"The number of immigrants," according to Mr. Marshall, "exceeded this capacity by 37 per cent."
Canada is no longer mainly an agricultural country. As a result of the war, we have
41-1	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Balcer taken a definite and permanent rank amongst industrial nations. We cannot get immigrants in equal numbers and of the same quality as in the past.
"In the present stage of our economic development," according to Mr. Stewart Bates, deputy minister of fisheries, "we do not need more farmers and fishermen; at best we need miners, labourers to engage in heavy work, servants, and so forth."
With all due respect to the minister of immigration.
I therefore suggest that unless we provide adequate shelter and housing to the working class, unless we secure those necessary markets for the sale of our farm products, unless our statutes provide sufficiently remunerative employment for hundreds of thousands of seasonally unemployed, unless our future as a nation is secured, we must approach the grave problem of immigration with extreme care.
Our country will not grow if we import human cattle. It will grow if we protect the family, encourage the raising of children and provide every Canadian with a happy home where he may live in peace.
If Canada can support a larger population than at present, there is no reason why, with our rich heritage, we should have poverty, unemployment and misery in our midst.
No immigration as long as there is unemployment! No favours to any foreigners as long as our own people have not been provided with the daily bread they are fully entitled to! No privileges to refugees as long as the sons of the pioneers of our country have not been treated in the fair and equitable manner to which they are entitled! Positions, salaries, comforts, leisure and security should go to Canadians first. That is what we want and expect, because we are entitled to it. That is what thousands of unemployed from the constituency of Chicoutimi expect from the federal government.

speechtext:
At the beginning of this session, I am duty bound as member for the county of Three Rivers to deal first of all with the unemployment problem which affects so deeply our country and the St. Maurice district in particular.
As the member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon) stated so well a few moments ago, the number of unemployed is increasing daily. In spite of the optimism shown by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) the situation has become serious even though the government does not seem to realize it.
The situation must be examined seriously and the government must use all means at its disposal to remove or at least to mitigate the consequences.
My constituency is one of those that really have to suffer from this scourge.
The city of Three Rivers, with a population of fifty thousand, has about five thousand unemployed registered with the local employment office. According to experts there probably are another thousand unemployed who are not registered.
I do not claim that they are all heads of families, but their number is sufficient for the situation to have disastrous effects both on the commercial and the agricultural aspects of our national economy.
To the representations made, and rightly so, by the leader of our party in this connection, the government has answered that unemployment is only local and seasonal. But the whole country is only too well aware of the fact that such a situation prevails from coast to coast and that every province is affected by unemployment, a problem which the government considers as of a purely local nature.
The government seems astonished that our people should be concerned with the fact that there are approximately five hundred thousand jobless in this country.
The Liberal party finds it normal that there should be a certain number of unemployed every winter and that in various sections of the country 5, 10 or 15 per cent of the labour force should be without work. Its attitude was surely different prior to June 27.

The government should do everything humanly possible to remedy that deplorable state of affairs. In our opinion it has been remiss in its duty.
Every party in the house agrees that the scope of the Unemployment Insurance Act should be extended without delay. But such a move will only bring temporary and inadequate relief. What the jobless are requesting at present is the undertaking of public works in order to ensure prosperity in districts where there is unemployment. The large labour organizations of Canada are also pressing for such remedial action.
However the government refuses to undertake those public works, contending that unemployment is of a purely local and temporary character. That, Mr. Speaker, is a further argument in favour of those projects. If unemployment is of a local and temporary character, so are public works by their very nature.
In the city of Three Rivers, where there are at present almost 6,000 unemployed, a large scale program of public works should be carried out in order to ensure the future prosperity of the whole district. Our piers are in poor condition and new sheds are needed if Three Rivers is to remain one of the important seaports of the country.
In Three Rivers also, as in the other cities affected by unemployment, there are slums where large families have to live under conditions which from the health and social standpoint are disgraceful. In the 20th century, such a state of affairs is inexcusable in a country as wealthy as ours.
I honestly believe that there has never been a more auspicious time for the dominion government to sign an agreement with the provincial government and the municipality of Three Rivers in order to eliminate this scourge of society.
Another public project should be undertaken in our district; I refer to the building of a bridge on the St. Lawrence connecting Three Rivers and Ste. Angele. Between Montreal and Quebec, no bridge crosses this mighty river. A bridge there would serve some ten counties and would help eliminate unemployment in that area for several years to come.
In this connection I should like to quote an editorial from the Three Rivers he Nouvelliste of Saturday, February 25th last. This editorial, headed "Bridge claimed' by St. Maurice valley city councils", reads as follows:
Mayors and aldermen of the city councils of the St. Maurice valley, who are to meet in the city
The Address-Mr. Balcer of Shawinigan today, will be asked to vote upon a resolution requesting the federal authorities to expedite the building of a bridge over the St. Lawrence, between Three Rivers and the south shore, as a measure to alleviate unemployment, which is growing more and more serious in this area.
We are convinced that this resolution will be unanimously approved by all members present at this second meeting of the municipal authorities of the St. Maurice valley. In fact, the building of a bridge between the two shores of the river would be an excellent way of providing, for several years, regular employment to thousands of persons, especially common labourers, who always suffer most whenever such seasonal unemployment as we are now experiencing occurs. It would most assuredly be a sane and highly beneficial measure which would furnish remunerative employment to thousands of people.
Besides helping ease the unemployment, the building of a bridge over the St. Lawrence is needed to ensure quick and easy communications between St. Maurice river valley, the south shore of the St. Lawrence and the United States. Nowadays there is more talk than ever before of completing the Three Rivers-Megantic highway and of extending it to the American border in the state of Maine. To achieve all these hoped for results, this project requires the bridging of the St. Lawrence.
There has been much talk of this project in the past and federal authorities are well acquainted with it. A few years ago almost every municipality on both shores of the St. Lawrence forwarded resolutions to the responsible authorities requesting that the building of this bridge be proceeded with. We were then at war and it was said that the proposal might be taken up as a post-war public works project.
The war, Mr. Speaker, has been over for five years, and it is time the government did something about this.
I also wish to take this opportunity to request the building of a post office in the municipality of Yamachiche. Yamachiche is today a rural mail distribution centre for several neighbouring parishes and such a building would be very useful.
In another sphere, a field of action in which federal aid would really be appropriate is the building of waterworks in the rural municipalities in my constituency. This would be an excellent means of helping the rural unemployed, while at the same time ensuring a sanitary running water distribution system and adequate protection against fires in the beautiful rural parishes of our county. These rural parishes are already suffering seriously from the loss of our agricultural markets and such federal aid would help to lighten the burden.
I have mentioned but a few of the public works which should be undertaken by the government to help the unemployed in my constituency. I could list many more if the government were ready to undertake them.

The Address-Mr. Balcer
To date, only one solution has been found by the government: let the municipalities concerned find work for their unemployed.
This is a very strange way of meeting problems and dodging responsibilities. For the people know very well that of all the taxes collected in Canada 76 per cent find their way into the federal treasury, whereas the provinces and municipalities must be satisfied with the balance, that is 24 per cent.
What can the municipalities do with scarcely 10 per cent of the taxes? It is physically impossible for them to solve the unemployment problem without any assistance from the government which grabs the lion's share of revenues, while refusing to shoulder its responsibilities.
As far as the government is concerned, the present unemployment situation may be local and temporary. All the more reason why every effort should be made to prevent it from spreading any further. The most logical way would be to implement a public works program designed to promote the future prosperity of the communities most affected.
And now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with another timely matter, although along a different line of thought.
It is unfortunate that the speech from the throne has no provision for the purpose of endowing our country with a truly national and a truly Canadian flag. Such a provision would have met the wish of people from every province.
Under the present government, our country seems to suffer from an inferiority complex. Every country in the world has had a flag of its own for centuries. In the government's opinion, Canada is not yet mature enough to have a token of the spirit of our nation.
We have recently been through a world war that brought glory to our troops, but our soldiers, sailors and airmen never knew under what flag they were fighting. Since the war, our Department of External Affairs has opened more than fifty embassies, legations and general consulates throughout the world. Yet our representatives have no flag to hoist on the masts of their embassy. There are in Canada thousands of public buildings erected with funds supplied by our fellow citizens. We are unable to raise on those buildings a flag that would arouse in the minds of our people a true Canadian spirit.
In all our schools, from the smallest rural school to our large universities, devoted teachers are trying hard to instil in our young people a feeling of national pride.


At present, our department of immigration spares no effort to inform thousands of new Canadians about the country and its glorious history.
The government, however, in spite of the majority which its supporters never fail to mention, hesitates to give every Canadian a symbol that would fill them with justifiable pride.
Such an emblem should be free of all colonial ties which would not be suitable to an independent country like ours.
The Canadian flag should be neither English, French nor Ukrainian, but Canadian. Thus it would strengthen national unity which must rest upon the legitimate pride all citizens feel for their great country. The fact that our ancestors were French, English or Polish does not in any way prevent us from being Canadians above all else.
There is at present, a movement which has gained in popularity all over the country. It is called the ligue du drapeau national. It advocates a truly Canadian emblem, in keeping with heraldic requirements and of such a design which, embodying a neatly contrasting maple leaf, would be acceptable to all true Canadians.
I therefore urge the government to make a gesture of national import and adopt this flag without delay.

However, trusting that the members of the house will bear with me, I already feel much better and I promise to deliver the message of the electors of the beautiful constituency of Kamouraska, a constituency remarkable for political clashes and for the men who have represented it since confederation. Among others, I am pleased to mention the name of one who was a disciple of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and the father of the Solicitor General of Canada, the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe whose name, after a quarter of a century, still holds first place in the affections of the Liberals of my constituency.
Mr. Speaker, after having listened to the debates that have taken place here, I can but congratulate you upon the dignity and impartiality with which you carry out the tasks that devolve upon you. You seem to have an innate sense of what is right, proper and reasonable.

Along with all those who have spoken before me, I wish to congratulate both the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the hon. members for Kindersley and Villeneuve (Messrs. I will not dwell at any length upon a description of the constituency of Kamour-aska, which is well known to the members of this house. I might however remind them that it is bounded on the north by the St. Lawrence river, on the south by the American border, on the east by the constituency of Temiscouata and on the west by Montmagny-L'lslet.
